docs.snippet: You can build, run, and test your Worker code on your own local machine before deploying it to Cloudflare's network. This is made possible through Miniflare, a simulator that executes your Worker code using the same runtime used in production, workerd ↗.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: With Cloudflare Access, you can restrict who is authorized to access your application. You decide who is approved, and every request is checked before your Worker runs. Approved visitors are let through, while everyone else is shown a login page or blocked.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Require sign-in on every Worker in your account, including Workers you deploy in the future. You can require sign-in on only preview deployments, or on both production and preview deployments.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Policy options

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When you turn on Access, choose who can sign in. The same policy options are available whether you protect all Workers or one Worker.

docs.snippet: When Cloudflare Access authenticates a request that directly invokes your Worker, the Worker can read the signed-in user's identity — including email, groups, device posture, and more identity fields — through ctx.access. No extra configuration or JWT parsing is required.

docs.title: `ctx.access` limitations

docs.snippet: Compatibility flags enable specific features. They can be useful if you want to help the Workers team test upcoming changes that are not yet enabled by default, or if you need to hold back a change that your code depends on but still want to apply other compatibility changes.

docs.title: Setting compatibility flags
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Setting compatibility flags
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You may provide a list of compatibility_flags, which enable or disable specific changes.

docs.title: Via Wrangler
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Setting compatibility flags > Via Wrangler
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This example enables the specific flag formdata_parser_supports_files, which is described below. As of the specified date, 2021-09-14, this particular flag was not yet enabled by default, but, by specifying it in compatibility_flags, we can enable it anyway. compatibility_flags…

docs.title: Via the Cloudflare Dashboard
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Setting compatibility flags > Via the Cloudflare Dashboard
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Compatibility flags can be updated in the Workers settings on the Cloudflare dashboard ↗.

docs.title: Via the Cloudflare API
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Setting compatibility flags > Via the Cloudflare API
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Compatibility flags can be set when uploading a Worker using the Workers Script API or Workers Versions API in the request body's metadata field.

docs.title: Node.js compatibility flag
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Node.js compatibility flag
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The nodejs\_compat flag also enables nodejs_compat_v2 for compatibility dates from 2024-09-23 through 2026-08-03. The v2 flag improves Node.js compatibility by bundling additional polyfills and globals into your Worker. However, this improvement increases bundle size.

docs.title: Remove Node.js 24.x end-of-life APIs
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Remove Node.js 24.x end-of-life APIs
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When remove_nodejs_compat_eol_v24 is enabled, APIs that reached end-of-life in Node.js 24.x are removed.

docs.title: Remove Node.js 22.x end-of-life APIs
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Remove Node.js 22.x end-of-life APIs
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When remove_nodejs_compat_eol_v22 is enabled, APIs that reached end-of-life in Node.js 22.x are removed.

docs.title: Throw On Not Implements TLS Options
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Throw On Not Implements TLS Options
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enabled, passing unsupported TLS options (e.g. checkServerIdentity) to tls.connect() or new TLSSocket() throws ERR_OPTION_NOT_IMPLEMENTED instead of silently ignoring them

docs.title: Process .pth files for Python Workers
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Process .pth files for Python Workers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When the python_process_pth_files flag is set, Python Workers process .pthfiles in the python_modules/ directory during startup by calling site.addsitedir() ↗on it. This lets packages extend sys.path declaratively, for example to add subdirectories or register import hooks.…

docs.title: Node.js diagnostics\_channel hasSubscribers getter
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Node.js diagnostics\_channel hasSubscribers getter
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When diagnostics_channel_has_subscribers_getter is enabled, Channel.hasSubscribers and TracingChannel.hasSubscribers from node:diagnostics_channel become read-only getter properties that evaluate directly to a boolean, matching Node.js behavior.

docs.title: Workflows preserve `NonRetryableError` message
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Workflows preserve `NonRetryableError` message
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enabled, if a Workflow step throws a NonRetryableError, the error message and name properties are preserved on the thrown exception instead of being replaced with a generic termination string.

docs.title: Enhanced error serialization
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enhanced error serialization
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enhanced_error_serialization is enabled, errors serialized using structuredClone() or V8 serialization support more error types and include own properties on the error object.

docs.title: Use an isolated PID namespace for containers
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Use an isolated PID namespace for containers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When containers_pid_namespace is set, containers will use an isolated PID namespace. The ENTRYPOINT of your container will have PID 1.

docs.title: Spec-compliant TextEncoderStream/TextDecoderStream backpressure
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Spec-compliant TextEncoderStream/TextDecoderStream backpressure
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When encoder_stream_spec_compliant_backpressure is enabled, TextEncoderStream and TextDecoderStream use a readable-side high water mark of 0, as specified by the WHATWG Encoding Standard ↗.

docs.title: Spec-compliant WritableStream writer behavior
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Spec-compliant WritableStream writer behavior
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When writable_stream_spec_compliant_writer is enabled, several WritableStream spec compliance issues around writer lock and release behavior are fixed to match the WHATWG Streams Standard ↗.

docs.title: Enable global Performance classes
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable global Performance classes
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enable_global_performance_classes is enabled, the following classes are available on the global scope: PerformanceEntry, PerformanceMark, PerformanceMeasure, PerformanceResourceTiming, PerformanceObserver, and PerformanceObserverEntryList.

docs.title: Enable `node:child_process` module
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `node:child_process` module
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_child_process_module flag enables the node:child_process module stub in Workers.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_perf_hooks_module flag enables the node:perf_hooks module in Workers. This flag also implicitly enables global Performance classes (PerformanceEntry, PerformanceMark, PerformanceMeasure, PerformanceResourceTiming, PerformanceObserver, and…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_readline_module flag enables the node:readline module stub in Workers.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This flag is automatically enabled for Workers using a compatibility date of 2026-03-17 or later when nodejs\_compat is enabled.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This flag is automatically enabled for Workers using a compatibility date of 2026-03-17 or later when nodejs\_compat is enabled.

docs.title: Enable `node:worker_threads` module
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `node:worker_threads` module
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_worker_threads_module flag enables the node:worker_threads module stub in Workers.

docs.title: WebSocket standard binary type
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > WebSocket standard binary type
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This flag controls the default value of the binaryType property on WebSocket, which in turn controls how binary frames are delivered to the message event. With the flag active, binaryType defaults to "blob" and binary frames arrive as Blob ↗ objects, matching the WebSocket…

docs.title: Expose error codes in Queue operations
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Expose error codes in Queue operations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When queue_expose_error_codes is enabled, Queue operations will include detailed error information, including error codes and causes, making it easier to handle and diagnose queue-related errors programmatically.

docs.title: WebSocket auto-reply to close
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > WebSocket auto-reply to close
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When a server sends a WebSocket Close frame, the Workers runtime now automatically sends a reciprocal Close frame and transitions readyState to CLOSED before firing the close event. This matches the WebSocket spec ↗ and browser behavior.

docs.title: Dedicated CJK TextDecoder implementation
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Dedicated CJK TextDecoder implementation
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When text_decoder_cjk_decoder is enabled, a dedicated CJK TextDecoder implementation is used for CJK encoding overrides and Big5 lead-byte handling, instead of the legacy ICU-only code path. This improves spec compliance for CJK text decoding.

docs.title: Defer unhandled rejection processing to after microtask checkpoint
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Defer unhandled rejection processing to after microtask checkpoint
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When unhandled_rejection_after_microtask_checkpoint is enabled, unhandledrejection event processing is deferred until the microtask checkpoint completes. This avoids misfires on multi-tick promise chains where a rejection handler is added in a later microtask.

docs.title: Enforce WebSocket close reason byte limit
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enforce WebSocket close reason byte limit
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When websocket_close_reason_byte_limit is enabled, WebSocket.close() throws a SyntaxError DOMException if the reason string exceeds 123 bytes when UTF-8 encoded, as required by the WHATWG WebSocket spec ↗ and RFC 6455 Section 5.5 ↗.

docs.title: Durable Object `deleteAll()` deletes alarms
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Durable Object `deleteAll()` deletes alarms
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: With the delete_all_deletes_alarm flag set, calling deleteAll() on a Durable Object's storage will delete any active alarm in addition to all stored data. Previously, deleteAll() only deleted user-stored data, and alarms required a separate deleteAlarm() call to remove. This…

docs.title: TextDecoder replaces lone surrogates
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > TextDecoder replaces lone surrogates
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When text_decoder_replace_surrogates is enabled, the UTF-16le TextDecoder will replace lone surrogates with U+FFFD (the Unicode replacement character) as required by the Encoding Standard ↗. Previously, lone surrogates were passed through unchanged, producing non-well-formed…

docs.title: Support iterables as fetch Request/Response body
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Support iterables as fetch Request/Response body
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When fetch_iterable_type_support is enabled, sync and async iterables can be passed as the body of a fetch() Request or Response and will be properly iterated over.

docs.title: Enable Node.js-compatible global timers
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable Node.js-compatible global timers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enable_nodejs_global_timers is enabled, setTimeout, setInterval, clearTimeout, and clearInterval return Node.js-compatible Timeout objects with methods like refresh(), ref(), unref(), and hasRef(), matching the behavior of node:timers.

docs.title: Enable `node:dgram` module
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `node:dgram` module
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_dgram_module flag enables the node:dgram module stub in Workers.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Enable `node:_stream_wrap` module
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `node:_stream_wrap` module
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_stream_wrap_module flag enables the node:_stream_wrap module stub in Workers.

docs.title: `require()` returns default export
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > `require()` returns default export
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When require_returns_default_export is enabled, require() will return the default export of a module if it exists. If the default export does not exist, it falls back to returning a mutable copy of the module namespace object.

docs.title: Duplicate stubs in RPC params instead of transferring ownership
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Duplicate stubs in RPC params instead of transferring ownership
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Changes the ownership semantics of RPC stubs embedded in the parameters of an RPC call, fixing compatibility issues with Cap'n Web ↗.

docs.title: Fetch iterable body respects toString/toPrimitive overrides

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When fetch_iterable_type_support_override_adjustment is enabled, objects passed as the body of a fetch() Request or Response that are sync iterable but also have a custom toString or Symbol.toPrimitive method will not be treated as iterables. Instead, they will fall through to…

docs.title: Strip UTF-8 BOM in stream `readAllText()`
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Strip UTF-8 BOM in stream `readAllText()`
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When strip_bom_in_read_all_text is enabled, the readAllText() method on streams will strip a leading UTF-8 Byte Order Mark (BOM) if present, matching the expected behavior per web platform standards.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_cluster_module flag enables the node:cluster module stub in Workers.

docs.title: Enable `node:punycode` module
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `node:punycode` module
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Enable `node:wasi` module

docs.title: Enable fast JSG struct optimization
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable fast JSG struct optimization
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enable_fast_jsg_struct is enabled, internal struct types used by Workers runtime APIs are constructed using a more efficient pattern that reduces object creation time.

docs.title: Enable ctx.exports
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable ctx.exports
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This flag enables the ctx.exports API, which contains automatically-configured loopback bindings for your Worker's top-level exports. This allows you to skip configuring explicit bindings for your WorkerEntrypoints and Durable Object namespaces defined in the same Worker.

docs.title: Enable `node:console` module

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_console_module flag enables the node:console module in Workers.

docs.title: Enable workflow entrypoint validation
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable workflow entrypoint validation
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enable_validate_workflow_entrypoint is enabled, additional validation checks are performed to ensure that Workflows are defined and used correctly. This helps catch configuration errors at upload time rather than at runtime.

docs.title: Enable `node:fs` module
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `node:fs` module
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This flag is automatically enabled for Workers using a compatibility date of 2025-09-15 or later when nodejs\_compat is enabled.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When enabled after 2025-09-15, the enable_nodejs_process_v2 flag along with the nodejs\_compat compat flag ensures a comprehensive Node.js-compatible process implementation, updating from the previous minimal process implementation that only provided the limited nextTick, env,…

docs.title: Enable Node.js HTTP server modules

docs.title: Remove end-of-life Node.js APIs

docs.snippet: When remove_nodejs_compat_eol is enabled, APIs that have reached End-of-Life in Node.js will be removed for Workers. When disabled, the APIs are present but might still be non-functional stubs.

docs.title: Remove Node.js 23.x end-of-life APIs

docs.snippet: When remove_nodejs_compat_eol_v23 is enabled, APIs that reached end-of-life in Node.js 23.x (EOL June 2025) are removed.

docs.title: Strip Authorization header on cross-origin redirects
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Strip Authorization header on cross-origin redirects
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When strip_authorization_on_cross_origin_redirect is enabled, the Authorization header is automatically removed when following a redirect to a different origin. This behavior is required by the current Fetch API specification ↗.

docs.title: Enable availability of `node:http` and `node:https` modules
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable availability of `node:http` and `node:https` modules
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The enable_nodejs_http_modules flag enables the availability of Node.js node:http and node:https modules in Workers (client APIS only).

docs.title: Expose global MessageChannel and MessagePort
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Expose global MessageChannel and MessagePort
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When the expose_global_message_channel flag is set, Workers will expose the MessageChannel and MessagePort constructors globally.

docs.title: Disable global handlers for Python Workers
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Disable global handlers for Python Workers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When the python_no_global_handlers flag is set, Python Workers will disable the global handlers and enforce their use via default entrypoint classes.

docs.title: Set the `this` value of EventTarget event handlers
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Set the `this` value of EventTarget event handlers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When the set_event_target_this flag is se, Workers will set the this value of event handlers to the EventTarget instance that the event is being dispatched on. This is compliant with the specification.

docs.title: Set forwardable email full headers
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Set forwardable email full headers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The original version of the headers sent to edgeworker were truncated to a single value for specific header names, such as To and Cc. With the set_forwardable_email_full_headers flag set, Workers will receive the full header values to the worker script.

docs.title: Pedantic Web Platform Tests (WPT) compliance
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Pedantic Web Platform Tests (WPT) compliance
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The pedantic_wpt flag enables strict compliance with Web Platform Tests (WPT) in Workers. Initially this only effects Event and EventTarget APIs but will be expanded to other APIs in the future. There is no default enable date for this flag.

docs.title: Bind AsyncLocalStorage snapshots to the request
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Bind AsyncLocalStorage snapshots to the request
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The AsyncLocalStorage frame can capture values that are bound to the current request context. This is not always in the users control since we use the ALS storage frame to propagate internal trace spans as well as user-provided values. When the…

docs.title: Throw on unrecognized import assertions
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Throw on unrecognized import assertions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The throw_on_unrecognized_import_assertion flag controls how Workers handle import attributes that are not recognized by the runtime. Previously, Workers would ignore all import attributes, which is not compliant with the specification. Runtimes are expected to throw an error…

docs.title: Enable eval during startup
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable eval during startup
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When the allow_eval_during_startup flag is set, Workers can use eval()and new Function(text) during the startup phase of a Worker script. This allows for dynamic code execution at the beginning of a Worker lifecycle.

docs.title: Enable `Request.signal` for incoming requests
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `Request.signal` for incoming requests
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When you use the enable_request_signal compatibility flag, you can attach an event listener to Request objects, using the signal property ↗. This allows you to perform tasks when the request to your Worker is canceled by the client.

docs.title: Cache API request `cf` overrides cache rules
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Cache API request `cf` overrides cache rules
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When cache_api_request_cf_overrides_cache_rules is enabled, cache settings specified in the cf object of a request passed to the Cache API will override cache rules. This applies only to user-owned or grey-clouded sites.

docs.title: Enable `navigator.language`
docs.heading_path: Compatibility flags > Flags history > Enable `navigator.language`
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When the enable_navigator_language flag is set, the navigator.language property will be available in Workers. For now, the value of navigator.language will always be en.

docs.title: Disallowing importable environment

docs.title: Placement
docs.heading_path: Placement
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, Workers and Pages Functions run in a data center closest to where the request was received. If your Worker makes requests to back-end infrastructure such as databases or APIs, it may be more performant to run that Worker closer to your back-end than the end user.

docs.heading_path: Placement > Understand placement
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Consider a user in Sydney, Australia accessing an application running on Workers. This application makes multiple round trips to a database in Frankfurt, Germany.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A version captures the complete state of your Worker at a point in time: its bundled code, static assets, bindings, and compatibility settings. Each version has a unique ID and tracks who created it, when, and from where.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A deployment determines which version(s) of your Worker are actively serving traffic. A deployment can reference one version (serving 100% of traffic) or two versions (with traffic split between them during a gradual deployment).

docs.title: Default behavior
docs.heading_path: Versions & deployments > Default behavior
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, these two concepts are coupled together - when you run wrangler deploy, Workers creates a new version and immediately deploys it to 100% of traffic in a single step.

docs.title: Version skew
docs.heading_path: Gradual deployments > Version skew
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Because gradual deployments mean multiple versions of your Worker serve traffic simultaneously, clients and services can end up interacting with more than one version in ways that produce errors or inconsistent behavior. This is called **version skew**.

docs.title: Version skew within a Worker
docs.heading_path: Gradual deployments > Version skew > Version skew within a Worker
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, each request is independently routed to a version based on the configured percentages. This means consecutive requests from the same user - including page reloads and asset fetches - can be handled by different versions.

docs.title: Version skew between Workers
docs.heading_path: Gradual deployments > Version skew > Version skew between Workers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When one Worker calls another via a service binding, the two Workers may be at different points in their own gradual deployment. Worker A (on its new version) might call Worker B, but the request lands on Worker B's old version where the API contract is different.

docs.title: Durable Objects

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Gradual deployments work differently for Durable Objects because only one version of each Durable Object can run at a time. Refer to Gradual Deployments with Durable Objects for details on version assignment, guarantees, and migrations.

docs.title: Version affinity
docs.heading_path: Version affinity
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: During a gradual deployment, each request has a random chance of routing to either version based on the specified percentages. This means the same user can be served content from a different version every time a request is made, which can cause **version skew** issues.

docs.title: How it works
docs.heading_path: Version affinity > How it works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Set the Cloudflare-Workers-Version-Key header on the incoming request to your Worker:

docs.title: Static assets
docs.heading_path: Version affinity > Static assets
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Version affinity is particularly important when your Worker serves static assets with content-hashed filenames (like index-a1b2c3d4.js), which is the default behavior of most modern build tools and frameworks.

docs.title: Choose a version key
docs.heading_path: Version affinity > Choose a version key
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The right version key depends on what stable identifiers your application has available. You can set the header using a Transform Rule on your zone, which extracts values from the request without modifying your application code.

docs.title: Authenticated applications
docs.heading_path: Version affinity > Choose a version key > Authenticated applications
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If your application has a user identifier in a cookie or header, this is the best option. Each user is deterministically assigned to a version and stays there across sessions, devices, and reloads.

docs.title: Applications with sessions
docs.heading_path: Version affinity > Choose a version key > Applications with sessions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If your application sets a session cookie, use the session identifier. This gives consistent routing for the duration of the session. If the session expires and a new one is created, the user may be assigned to a different version.

docs.title: Workers Cache
docs.heading_path: Workers Cache
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Workers Cache lets Cloudflare return cached HTTP responses from your Worker without executing your Worker code. When an incoming request matches a cached response, Cloudflare serves the response directly from its edge cache — reducing latency and Workers CPU usage.

docs.title: Your Worker's cache
docs.heading_path: Workers Cache > Your Worker's cache
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Workers Cache is **your Worker's cache**. It is owned by your Worker, operated by your Worker, and private to your Worker.

docs.title: The Worker is the configuration surface
docs.heading_path: Workers Cache > Your Worker's cache > The Worker is the configuration surface
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A Worker is **already infinitely customizable**. You can change response bodies, rewrite headers, branch on any request attribute, call out to other Workers via service bindings or ctx.exports, and compose logic across an entire system.

docs.title: When caching helps
docs.heading_path: Workers Cache > When caching helps
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Perform CPU-intensive work whose result can be reused across requests — content generation, template rendering, data transformation. * Fetch data from a slow origin or third-party API and want to absorb that latency for subsequent requests. * Power a server-rendered or…

docs.title: How it works
docs.heading_path: Workers Cache > How it works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: With caching enabled, Cloudflare checks the cache before running your Worker. On a hit, the cached response is returned directly. On a miss, your Worker runs, and if the response is cacheable per its Cache-Control header, Cloudflare stores it for the next request.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.heading_path: Limitations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This page lists the scenarios where Workers Caching does not apply, followed by notes on how it relates to other caches you may already be using.

docs.title: HTTP methods
docs.heading_path: Limitations > Unsupported scenarios > HTTP methods
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Only GET and HEAD requests are cached. POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, and other methods always invoke your Worker.

docs.title: WebSocket upgrades
docs.heading_path: Limitations > Unsupported scenarios > WebSocket upgrades
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: WebSocket upgrade requests (GET with Upgrade: websocket) bypass the cache and always invoke your Worker. WebSocket sessions are stateful by definition and are not a meaningful unit of caching.

docs.title: Custom RPC methods
docs.heading_path: Limitations > Unsupported scenarios > Custom RPC methods
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Only fetch() invocations on a WorkerEntrypoint go through Workers Caching. Custom RPC methods like ctx.exports.Backend.getUser(id) bypass the cache and always run the callee, regardless of the entrypoint's cache.enabled setting.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Workers Caching only applies to HTTP requests handled by a fetch handler on a Worker entrypoint. The following invocation types always run without cache involvement:

docs.title: Purge by host
docs.heading_path: Limitations > Unsupported scenarios > Purge by host
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: There is no "purge by host" mode. The cache belongs to the Worker, not to a domain — the host is not part of the cache key, so purging by host would not map onto anything the cache stores. Use purge by tag, purge by path prefix, or purgeEverything instead.

docs.title: Cache pre-warming
docs.heading_path: Limitations > Unsupported scenarios > Cache pre-warming
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: There is no API to pre-populate the cache with responses generated at build time. A response is only cached once it has been served at least once. If you need pre-rendered content available to the first requester, use Static Assets.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Response size limits are the same as Cloudflare's zone cache. For per-plan limits, refer to Cacheable size limits.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When your Worker finishes processing a request, the database client is automatically garbage collected and the edge connection to Hyperdrive is cleaned up. Hyperdrive keeps the underlying connection to your origin database open in its pool for reuse.

docs.title: Cleaning up client connections

docs.snippet: You should always create database clients inside your request handlers (fetch, queue, and similar), not in the global scope. Workers do not allow I/O across requests, and Hyperdrive's distributed connection pooling already solves for connection startup latency. Using a…

docs.snippet: Unlike regular Workers, Durable Objects can maintain state across multiple requests. If you keep a database client open in a Durable Object, the connection will remain allocated from Hyperdrive's connection pool. Long-lived Durable Objects can exhaust available connections if…

docs.snippet: The Hyperdrive connection pooler operates in transaction mode, where the client that executes the query communicates through a single connection for the duration of a transaction. When that transaction has completed, the connection is returned to the pool.

docs.title: Query caching
docs.heading_path: Query caching
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Hyperdrive automatically caches cacheable read queries that your Worker sends to your database when query caching is turned on. This reduces database load and avoids a network round trip to your database for popular queries. Query caching is enabled by default.

docs.title: What does Hyperdrive cache?
docs.heading_path: Query caching > What does Hyperdrive cache?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Hyperdrive uses database protocols to differentiate between a mutating query (a query that writes to the database) and a non-mutating query (a read-only query). Hyperdrive caches eligible read-only query responses and does not cache writes.

docs.title: What does Hyperdrive cache?
docs.heading_path: Query caching > What does Hyperdrive cache?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: -- Not cached: NOW() returns a non-deterministic value SELECT * FROM events WHERE created_at > NOW() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR;

docs.title: What does Hyperdrive cache?
docs.heading_path: Query caching > What does Hyperdrive cache?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A: /* some text here */ SELECT * FROM some_table;B: /* some different text here */ SELECT * FROM some_table;

docs.title: Default cache settings
docs.heading_path: Query caching > Default cache settings
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The max_age setting determines the maximum lifetime a query response will be served from cache. Cached responses may be evicted from the cache prior to this time if they are rarely used.

docs.title: Read-after-write behavior
docs.heading_path: Query caching > Read-after-write behavior
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Hyperdrive does not purge or invalidate cached read query results when your application writes to your database. A later matching SELECT can return the cached result until the configured max_age expires. Hyperdrive can also serve the result during the stale_while_revalidate…

docs.title: Disable caching

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Disable caching on a per-Hyperdrive configuration basis by using the Wrangler CLI to set the --caching-disabled option.

docs.snippet: Hyperdrive can securely connect to your private databases using Cloudflare Tunnel and Cloudflare Access.

docs.title: How it works

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When your database is isolated within a private network (such as a virtual private cloud ↗ or an on-premise network), you must enable a secure connection from your network to Cloudflare.

docs.title: Before you start

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: All of the tutorials assume you have already completed the Get started guide, which gets you set up with a Cloudflare Workers account, C3 ↗, and Wrangler.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * A database in your private network, configured to use TLS/SSL. * A hostname on your Cloudflare account, which will be used to route requests to your database.

docs.title: 1.1\. Create a tunnel
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Tunnel > 1\. Create a tunnel in your private network > 1.1\. Create a tunnel
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: First, create a Cloudflare Tunnel in your private network to establish a secure connection between your network and Cloudflare. Your network must be configured such that the tunnel has permissions to egress to the Cloudflare network and access the database within your network.

docs.title: 1.2\. Connect your database using a public hostname
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Tunnel > 1\. Create a tunnel in your private network > 1.2\. Connect your database using a public hostname
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Your tunnel must be configured to use a public hostname on Cloudflare so that Hyperdrive can route requests to it. If you don't have a hostname on Cloudflare yet, you will need to register a new hostname or add a zone to Cloudflare to proceed.

docs.title: 2\. Create and configure Hyperdrive to connect to the Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Tunnel > 2\. Create and configure Hyperdrive to connect to the Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To restrict access to the Cloudflare Tunnel to Hyperdrive, a Cloudflare Access application must be configured with a Policy that requires requests to contain a valid Service Auth token.

docs.title: 2.1\. (Automatic) Create a Hyperdrive configuration in the Cloudflare dashboard
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Tunnel > 2\. Create and configure Hyperdrive to connect to the Cloudflare Tunnel > 2.1\. (Automatic) Create a Hyperdrive configuration in the Cloudflare dashboard
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Create a Hyperdrive configuration in the Cloudflare dashboard to automatically configure Hyperdrive to connect to your Cloudflare Tunnel.

docs.title: 2.1\. (Manual) Create a service token
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Tunnel > 2\. Create and configure Hyperdrive to connect to the Cloudflare Tunnel > 2.1\. (Manual) Create a service token
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The service token will be used to restrict requests to the tunnel, and is needed for the next step.

docs.title: 2.2\. (Manual) Create an Access application to secure the tunnel
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Tunnel > 2\. Create and configure Hyperdrive to connect to the Cloudflare Tunnel > 2.2\. (Manual) Create an Access application to secure the tunnel
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare Access will be used to verify that requests to the tunnel originate from Hyperdrive using the service token created above.

docs.title: 2.3\. (Manual) Create a Hyperdrive configuration

docs.title: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended)
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Workers VPC provides a way to connect Hyperdrive to a private database without configuring Cloudflare Access applications or service tokens. Instead, you create a TCP VPC Service that points to your database and pass its service ID to Hyperdrive.

docs.title: How it works
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended) > How it works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When your database is isolated within a private network (such as a virtual private cloud ↗ or an on-premise network), you must enable a secure connection from your network to Cloudflare.

docs.title: Before you start

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: All of the tutorials assume you have already completed the Get started guide, which gets you set up with a Cloudflare Workers account, C3 ↗, and Wrangler.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended) > Prerequisites
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * A database in your private network, configured to use TLS/SSL. * A Cloudflare Tunnel running in a network that can reach your database. * The **Connectivity Directory Admin** role on your Cloudflare account to create VPC Services.

docs.title: 1\. Set up a Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended) > 1\. Set up a Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you do not already have a tunnel running in the same network as your database, create one.

docs.title: 2\. Create a TCP VPC Service
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended) > 2\. Create a TCP VPC Service
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Create a VPC Service of type tcp that points to your database. Set the --app-protocol flag to postgresql or mysql so that Hyperdrive can optimize connections.

docs.title: TLS certificate verification
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended) > 2\. Create a TCP VPC Service > TLS certificate verification
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Unlike Hyperdrive, which does not verify the origin server certificate by default, Workers VPC defaults to verify_full — it verifies both the certificate chain and the hostname. If your database uses a self-signed certificate or a certificate from a private certificate authority…

docs.title: 3\. Create a Hyperdrive configuration
docs.heading_path: Connect to a private database using Workers VPC (Recommended) > 3\. Create a Hyperdrive configuration
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Use the --service-id flag to point Hyperdrive at the VPC Service you created. When you use --service-id, you do not provide --origin-host, --origin-port, or --connection-string. Hyperdrive routes traffic through the VPC Service instead.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You must create a binding in your Wrangler configuration file for your Worker to connect to your Hyperdrive configuration. Bindings allow your Workers to access resources, like Hyperdrive, on the Cloudflare developer platform.

docs.title: Choose a data or storage product
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This guide describes the storage & database products available as part of Cloudflare Workers, including recommended use-cases and best practices.

docs.title: Choose a storage product
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Choose a storage product
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The following table maps our storage & database products to common industry terms as well as recommended use-cases:

docs.title: Choose a storage product
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Choose a storage product
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Choose a storage product
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Choose a storage product
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Applications can build on multiple storage & database products: for example, using Workers KV for session data; R2 for large file storage, media assets and user-uploaded files; and Hyperdrive to connect to a hosted Postgres or MySQL database.

docs.title: SQL database options
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > SQL database options
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: There are three options for SQL-based databases available when building applications with Workers.

docs.title: Session storage
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > SQL database options > Session storage
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: We recommend using Workers KV for storing session data, credentials (API keys), and/or configuration data. These are typically read at high rates (thousands of RPS or more), are not typically modified (within KV's 1 write RPS per unique key limit), and do not need to be…

docs.title: Workers KV
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Product overviews > Workers KV
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Workers KV is an eventually consistent key-value data store that caches on the Cloudflare global network.

docs.title: R2
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Product overviews > R2
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: R2 is S3-compatible blob storage that allows developers to store large amounts of unstructured data without egress fees associated with typical cloud storage services.

docs.title: Durable Objects
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Product overviews > Durable Objects
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Durable Objects provide low-latency coordination and consistent storage for the Workers platform through global uniqueness and a transactional storage API.

docs.title: D1
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Product overviews > D1
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: D1 is Cloudflare’s native serverless database. With D1, you can create a database by importing data or defining your tables and writing your queries within a Worker or through the API.

docs.title: Queues
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Product overviews > Queues
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare Queues allows developers to send and receive messages with guaranteed delivery. It integrates with Cloudflare Workers and offers at-least once delivery, message batching, and does not charge for egress bandwidth.

docs.title: Hyperdrive
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Product overviews > Hyperdrive
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Hyperdrive is a service that accelerates queries you make to MySQL and Postgres databases, making it faster to access your data from across the globe, irrespective of your users’ location.

docs.title: Pipelines
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Pipelines
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Pipelines is a streaming ingestion service that allows you to ingest high volumes of real time data, without managing any infrastructure.

docs.title: Analytics Engine
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Pipelines > Analytics Engine
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Analytics Engine is Cloudflare's time-series and metrics database that allows you to write unlimited-cardinality analytics at scale using a built-in API to write data points from Workers and query that data using SQL directly.

docs.title: Vectorize
docs.heading_path: Choose a data or storage product > Pipelines > Vectorize
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Vectorize is a globally distributed vector database that enables you to build full-stack, AI-powered applications with Cloudflare Workers and Workers AI.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Below you will find answers to our most commonly asked questions regarding Hyperdrive.

docs.title: Does Hyperdrive use specific IP addresses to connect to my database?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Connectivity > Does Hyperdrive use specific IP addresses to connect to my database?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Hyperdrive connects to your database using Cloudflare's IP address ranges ↗. These are shared by all Hyperdrive configurations and other Cloudflare products.

docs.title: Does Hyperdrive support connecting to D1 databases?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Connectivity > Does Hyperdrive support connecting to D1 databases?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Hyperdrive does not support D1 because D1 provides fast connectivity from Workers by design.

docs.title: Should I use Placement with Hyperdrive?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Connectivity > Should I use Placement with Hyperdrive?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes, if your Worker makes multiple queries per request. Placement runs your Worker near your database, reducing per-query latency from 20-30ms to 1-3ms. Hyperdrive handles connection pooling and setup. Placement reduces the network distance for query execution.

docs.title: Does Hyperdrive invalidate cached reads when I write to my database
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Caching > Does Hyperdrive invalidate cached reads when I write to my database
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: No. Hyperdrive does not invalidate cached read query results when your application writes to your database. A matching read can return a cached result until the configured max_age expires, and Hyperdrive can serve that result during the stale_while_revalidate window while it…

docs.title: Can I use Hyperdrive if some reads need read-after-write consistency
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Caching > Can I use Hyperdrive if some reads need read-after-write consistency
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes. Configure two Hyperdrive bindings to the same database: one with query caching enabled for reads that can tolerate short staleness, and one with query caching disabled for reads that must be fresh. The cache-disabled binding still gives you Hyperdrive's connection pooling…

docs.title: Is Hyperdrive available on the [Workers Free](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#workers) plan?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Pricing > Is Hyperdrive available on the [Workers Free](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/platform/pricing/#workers) plan?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Is Hyperdrive available on the Workers Free plan?

docs.title: Does Hyperdrive charge for additional compute?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Pricing > Does Hyperdrive charge for additional compute?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Hyperdrive itself does not charge for compute (CPU) or processing (wall clock) time. Workers querying Hyperdrive and computing results: for example, serializing results into JSON and/or issuing queries, are billed per Workers pricing.

docs.title: How much work can a D1 database do?
docs.heading_path: Limits > Frequently Asked Questions > How much work can a D1 database do?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: D1 is designed for horizontal scale out across multiple, smaller (10 GB) databases, such as per-user, per-tenant or per-entity databases. D1 allows you to build applications with thousands of databases at no extra cost, as the pricing is based only on query and storage costs.

docs.heading_path: Backups (Legacy)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: D1 has built-in support for creating and restoring backups of your databases with wrangler v3, including support for scheduled automatic backups and manual backup management.

docs.title: Automatic backups
docs.heading_path: Backups (Legacy) > Automatic backups
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: D1 automatically backs up your databases every hour on your behalf, and retains backups for 24 hours. Backups will block access to the DB while they are running. In most cases this should only be a second or two, and any requests that arrive during the backup will be queued.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Downloading a backup locally
docs.heading_path: Backups (Legacy) > Downloading a backup locally
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To download a backup locally, call wrangler d1 backup download <DATABASE_NAME> <BACKUP_ID>. Use wrangler d1 backup list <DATABASE_NAME> to list the available backups, including their IDs, for a given D1 database.

docs.title: Restoring a backup
docs.heading_path: Backups (Legacy) > Restoring a backup
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Restoring a backup will overwrite the existing version of your D1 database in-place. We recommend you make a manual backup before you restore a database, so that you have a backup to revert to if you accidentally restore the wrong backup or break your application.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: D1 itself does not charge for additional compute. Workers querying D1 and computing results: for example, serializing results into JSON and/or running queries, are billed per Workers pricing, in addition to your D1 specific usage.

docs.title: How much work can a D1 database do?
docs.heading_path: FAQs > Limits > How much work can a D1 database do?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: D1 is designed for horizontal scale out across multiple, smaller (10 GB) databases, such as per-user, per-tenant or per-entity databases. D1 allows you to build applications with thousands of databases at no extra cost, as the pricing is based only on query and storage costs.

docs.snippet: D1 allows you to define generated columns based on the values of one or more other columns, SQL functions, or even extracted JSON values.

docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare DNS offers a few different setup options. A primary setup (also known as full) is the most common and the only one available for Free or Pro plans. For details, refer to About. For more introductory context, refer to Concepts.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > Before you begin
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Create a Cloudflare account — If you have not already, sign up for a Cloudflare account. * Own a domain name — You need a registered domain (for example, example.com). If you do not have one, you can register a domain at-cost through Cloudflare Registrar ↗. Domains purchased…

docs.title: 1\. Add your domain to Cloudflare
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 1\. Add your domain to Cloudflare
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. Log in to the Cloudflare dashboard ↗.  Go to **Domains** ↗ 2. Select **Onboard a domain**. 3. Enter your apex domain (for example, example.com) and choose how you would like to add your DNS records. 4. Select **Continue** and choose a plan ↗.

docs.title: 2\. Review your DNS records
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 2\. Review your DNS records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Your DNS records must be accurate for your domain to work properly. If you don't know what DNS records are, consider the video below for a quick explanation.

docs.title: Common records
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 2\. Review your DNS records > Common records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Since the quick scan is not guaranteed to find all existing DNS records, you need to review your records, paying special attention to the following:

docs.title: Proxy status
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 2\. Review your DNS records > Proxy status
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * **Proxied** (orange cloud): web traffic goes through the Cloudflare network, which provides caching, DDoS protection, and other security features. * **DNS only** (gray cloud): Cloudflare returns the DNS record value but does not proxy traffic. Use this for CNAME records that…

docs.title: 3\. Change your nameservers
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 3\. Change your nameservers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Your domain will be assigned two authoritative Cloudflare nameservers. Nameservers are specialized servers that store your domain's DNS records and "answer" requests from browsers by providing the specific IP address needed to connect to your website.

docs.title: 3.1\. Get nameserver names
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 3\. Change your nameservers > 3.1\. Get nameserver names
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Your assigned nameservers are displayed as part of the onboarding flow. If you need to find them once again, go the zone **Overview** page.

docs.title: 3.2\. Log in to your registrar
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 3\. Change your nameservers > 3.2\. Log in to your registrar
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Log in to the admin account for your domain registrar. If you do not know your provider, use ICANN Lookup ↗.

docs.title: 3.3\. Turn off DNSSEC
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 3\. Change your nameservers > 3.3\. Turn off DNSSEC
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If your domain has DNSSEC1 active, you must turn it off at your registrar before replacing nameservers. Changing nameservers while DNSSEC is active can cause your domain to become unreachable. You can re-enable DNSSEC through Cloudflare after your domain is active.

docs.title: 3.4\. Update your registrar
docs.heading_path: Set up a primary zone (Full setup) > 3\. Change your nameservers > 3.4\. Update your registrar
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. Remove your existing authoritative nameservers. 2. Add the nameservers provided by Cloudflare. If their names are not **copied exactly**, your DNS will not resolve correctly.

docs.snippet: The scan is built upon a list of recurring patterns of DNS records **Type** and **Name**, that Cloudflare identifies as being used in existing active zones.

docs.title: Limitations

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Since it is still common that visitors type www.<DOMAIN> in their browsers expecting to reach the domain, zones will usually have a CNAME or an A record named www. This allows queries for www.<DOMAIN> to return the expected result.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This page provides information about some of the different types of DNS records that you can manage on Cloudflare. For guidance on how to add, edit, or delete DNS records, refer to Manage DNS records.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: At least one **IP address resolution** record is required for each domain on Cloudflare. These records are the only ones you can proxy through Cloudflare.

docs.title: A and AAAA

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A and AAAA records ↗ map a domain name to one or multiple IPv4 or IPv6 address(es).

docs.title: CNAME
docs.heading_path: DNS record types > IP address resolution > CNAME
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: CNAME records ↗ map a domain name to another (canonical) domain name. They can be used to resolve other record types present on the target domain name.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: These records are recommended regardless of whether your domain sends email messages. Creating secure email records ↗ can help protect your domain against email spoofing.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A Domain-based Message Authentication Reporting and Conformance (DMARC) record helps generate aggregate reports about your email traffic and provide clear instructions for how email receivers should treat non-conforming emails.

docs.heading_path: DNS record types > Specialized records > TXT
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: As the content of TXT records consist of one or more text strings delimited by double quotes ("), you might find a validation error if you add inconsistent quotation marks (for example, "this or "these" ones"). For new records, if you save your TXT content without any quotes,…

docs.title: CAA
docs.heading_path: DNS record types > Specialized records > CAA
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A Certificate Authority Authorization (CAA) record specifies which Certificate Authorities (CAs) are allowed to issue certificates for a domain.

docs.title: SRV
docs.heading_path: DNS record types > Specialized records > SRV
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A service record (SRV) ↗ specifies a host and port for specific services like voice over IP (VOIP), instant messaging, and more.

docs.snippet: Service Binding (SVCB) and HTTPS Service (HTTPS) records allow you to provide a client with information about how it should connect to a server upfront, without the need of an initial plaintext HTTP connection.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: SOA

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A start of authority (SOA) record stores information about your domain such as admin email address, when the domain was last updated, and more. Refer to What is a DNS SOA record ↗ for an example.

docs.title: NS
docs.heading_path: DNS record types > Specialized records > NS
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A nameserver (NS) record ↗ indicates which server should be used for authoritative DNS.

docs.title: Limits
docs.heading_path: DNS record types > Specialized records > NS > Limits
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When creating NS records, there are limits on the number of nameservers that can be associated with a single delegation name.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: DS and DNSKEY ↗ records help implement DNSSEC, which cryptographically signs DNS records to prevent domain spoofing.

docs.snippet: Cloudflare also supports other record types that are less common, such as URI, NAPTR, and certificate-related record types (SSHFP, TLSA, SMIMEA, and CERT). Refer to our blog post ↗ for more information.

docs.title: Shadowed records
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When you add an NS record to your zone, you create a **subdomain delegation**: you delegate authority for that subdomain (and everything below it) to another set of nameservers. Any record you keep at or below that delegation point is **shadowed**. It stays stored in your zone,…

docs.title: Why shadowed records matter
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Why shadowed records matter
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Because a delegation moves authority for a subdomain elsewhere, any record you place at or below it is not authoritative, even though it still appears in your zone. Consider this example:

docs.title: Glue records
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Glue records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A glue record is an A or AAAA record that some delegations need in order to work. Glue is required only when a delegation's nameserver hostname falls within the delegated zone itself. Most delegations point at nameservers in a different zone (for example, ns1.example.org for a…

docs.title: Unreachable glue records
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Unreachable glue records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A glue record becomes unreachable when a shallower delegation takes authority for the name the glue is meant to support. The shallower delegation (one closer to the zone apex, with fewer labels in its name) takes authority for everything below it, so your zone cannot serve the…

docs.title: Shadow metadata fields
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Shadow metadata fields
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Shadow metadata fields are returned in each record's meta object when applicable. They are computed on demand at read time and are never stored.

docs.title: `shadowed_by`
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Shadow metadata fields > `shadowed_by`
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Present on any record that is hidden by one or more NS delegations. The array contains the IDs of the NS records whose delegations shadow this record. Multiple IDs appear when several NS records share the same delegation name, or when delegations exist at more than one parent…

docs.title: `is_glue`
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Shadow metadata fields > `is_glue`
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Present and set to true on A or AAAA records whose name matches the target of one of the NS records that shadows them. These records are required glue for the delegation. Even though they are shadowed, they are still served: the parent zone includes them in the additional…

docs.title: `dead_glue`
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Shadow metadata fields > `dead_glue`
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Present and set to true on glue records that are never actually served, because a shallower delegation intercepts authority before the zone can answer for that name. A record with dead_glue: true also carries is_glue: true.

docs.title: `shadowed_records_count`
docs.heading_path: Shadowed records > Shadow metadata fields > `shadowed_records_count`
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Present on non-apex NS records that form a delegation. Reports how many records in the zone are shadowed by that delegation (records at or below the delegation name, excluding the delegation's own NS records and hidden records).

docs.title: Time to Live (TTL)
docs.heading_path: Time to Live (TTL)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: **Time to Live (TTL)** is a field on DNS records that controls how long each record is cached and — as a result — how long it takes for record updates to reach your end users.

docs.title: Proxied records
docs.heading_path: Time to Live (TTL) > Proxied records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, all proxied records have a TTL of **Auto**, which is set to 300 seconds. This value cannot be edited.

docs.title: Unproxied records
docs.heading_path: Time to Live (TTL) > Unproxied records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: For **DNS only** records, you can choose a TTL between **30 seconds** (Enterprise) or **60 seconds** (non-Enterprise) and **1 day**.

docs.title: Nameserver TTL
docs.heading_path: Time to Live (TTL) > Nameserver TTL
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Nameserver TTL is a separate feature and only affects Cloudflare nameservers and custom nameservers. For other NS records on your DNS records table, TTL is controlled by their respective TTL fields.

docs.title: Wildcard DNS records
docs.heading_path: Wildcard DNS records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Normal DNS records map a domain name to one or multiple IP addresses or other associated resources to a specific domain name (a one-to-many mapping). Wildcard DNS records allow you to have a many-to-many mapping, for example if you had hundreds or thousands of subdomains you…

docs.title: Create a Wildcard record
docs.heading_path: Wildcard DNS records > Create a Wildcard record
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To create a wildcard DNS record, create a DNS record with an * in the **Name** field.

docs.title: Wildcards are only supported on the first label
docs.heading_path: Wildcard DNS records > Create a Wildcard record > Aspects to consider > Wildcards are only supported on the first label
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This means that a hostname such as subdomain.*.example.com is not a wildcard on the level of the asterisk character. If you create a DNS record with that name, the asterisk is interpreted as the literal character * and not as the wildcard operator.

docs.title: Wildcards are multi-level by default
docs.heading_path: Wildcard DNS records > Create a Wildcard record > Aspects to consider > Wildcards are multi-level by default
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you create a DNS record on *.*.example.com, only the first asterisk is interpreted as a wildcard while the second one is interpreted as the literal * character. A record *.example.com is already multi-level by default, meaning it would cover abc.example.com as well as…

docs.title: Specific DNS records take precedence over wildcard records
docs.heading_path: Wildcard DNS records > Create a Wildcard record > Aspects to consider > Specific DNS records take precedence over wildcard records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A wildcard record applies only when no exact record exists at the queried name. If a record or delegation exists, the wildcard does not apply.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.heading_path: Wildcard DNS records > Limitations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you are using a CNAME setup (partial) for your DNS, Cloudflare does not automatically provision SSL/TLS certificates for your wildcard record.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Unexpected DNS records > acme\_challenge TXT records > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: These records are automatically created to allow Cloudflare edge certificates (universal, advanced, and backup) to be provisioned. _acme-challenge records are required by certificate authorities (CAs) so that they can verify your domain ownership before issuing the SSL/TLS…

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Unexpected DNS records > acme\_challenge TXT records > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: As these records are tied to the certificates, they cannot be deleted via the Cloudflare dashboard.

docs.title: Proxied records
