docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The sections below describe specific behaviors and expected outcomes when you have DNS records set to proxied. There may also be some limitations in specific scenarios.

docs.title: Predefined time to live
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > Proxied records > Predefined time to live
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, all proxied records have a time to live (TTL) of **Auto**, which is set to 300 seconds. This value cannot be edited.

docs.title: Mix proxied and unproxied
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > Proxied records > Mix proxied and unproxied
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you have multiple A or AAAA records on the same name and at least one of them is proxied, Cloudflare will treat all A or AAAA records on this name as being proxied.

docs.title: CNAME records
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > Proxied records > CNAME records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: With CNAME flattening, Cloudflare follows the CNAME chain to find the final IP address, helping DNS queries resolve faster. Proxied CNAME records are flattened by default, as they return Cloudflare anycast IPs.

docs.title: Protocol optimization
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > Proxied records > Protocol optimization
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: For proxied records, if your domain has HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 enabled and is also using Universal SSL, Cloudflare automatically generates HTTPS Service (HTTPS) records on the fly. These DNS records provide clients with information about how to connect to your server upfront, without…

docs.title: Request and response size limits
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > Proxied records > Request and response size limits
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare enforces size limits on proxied requests. These limits vary by plan and cannot be bypassed while traffic is proxied. For the full list of connection and request limits, refer to Connection limits.

docs.title: Connection timeouts
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > Proxied records > Connection timeouts
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare enforces a default Proxy Read Timeout between Cloudflare and your origin server. If your origin does not send an HTTP response within the defined time limit, Cloudflare returns a 524 error. Enterprise customers can increase the timeout value.

docs.title: DNS-only records
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > DNS-only records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When an A, AAAA, or CNAME record is **DNS-only** — shown as a gray cloud icon in the dashboard, also known as "gray-clouded" — DNS queries for these will resolve to the record's actual origin IP address, as described in the example.

docs.title: When to use DNS-only
docs.heading_path: Proxy status > DNS-only records > When to use DNS-only
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Certain DNS records should be DNS-only because the services they support are not compatible with Cloudflare's HTTP proxy. Common examples include email records, domain verification records, SaaS-hosted websites, and non-HTTP services.

docs.snippet: This page describes expected limitations when proxying DNS records. For further information about proxying, refer to How Cloudflare DNS works.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Only A, AAAA, and CNAME records that serve HTTP or HTTPS traffic can be proxied. Other DNS record types cannot be proxied.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Ports and protocols
docs.heading_path: Proxying limitations > Ports and protocols
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To proxy HTTP/HTTPS traffic on non-standard ports or to proxy a TCP or UDP based application, use Cloudflare Spectrum.

docs.title: Pending domains
docs.heading_path: Proxying limitations > Pending domains
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When you add a domain to Cloudflare, Cloudflare protection will be in a pending state until we can verify ownership. This could take up to 24 hours to complete.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This page lists common scenarios where DNS records should be proxied or set to DNS only, and describes aspects to keep in mind depending on your configuration. For background on how proxy status works, refer to Proxy status.

docs.title: Proxied records
docs.heading_path: Use cases > Proxied records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You should proxy all A, AAAA, and CNAME records that serve HTTP or HTTPS web traffic. This includes records for:

docs.title: Source IP changes
docs.heading_path: Use cases > Proxied records > Source IP changes
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Your origin server sees Cloudflare IP addresses as the source of all requests instead of the end-user's IP address. Applications that rely on the source IP for authentication, rate limiting, or geolocation will not function as expected without additional configuration.

docs.title: Client certificate (mTLS) validation
docs.heading_path: Use cases > Proxied records > Client certificate (mTLS) validation
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When a record is proxied, TLS terminates at Cloudflare's global network. Cloudflare establishes a separate TLS connection to your origin server. This means the origin never receives the end-user's client certificate during the TLS handshake. You can achieve mTLS through the…

docs.title: Header modifications
docs.heading_path: Use cases > Proxied records > Header modifications
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare adds and modifies HTTP request headers when proxying traffic, including headers for visitor IP identification, diagnostics, and connection management. Applications that expect a fixed number of headers or parse headers by position instead of by name may experience…

docs.title: DNS only
docs.heading_path: Use cases > DNS only
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The following records should be set to DNS-only because the services they support are not compatible with Cloudflare's HTTP proxy. Proxying these records causes the associated service to break.

docs.title: Email
docs.heading_path: Use cases > DNS only > Email
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: MX records cannot be proxied. If an A or AAAA record is used exclusively for email (for example, mail.example.com), it should also be set to DNS-only.

docs.title: Domain verification
docs.heading_path: Use cases > DNS only > Domain verification
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Third-party services often require CNAME or TXT records to verify domain ownership. Proxying a verification CNAME record returns Cloudflare IP addresses instead of the expected verification target. The third-party service cannot match the response and verification fails.

docs.title: SaaS-hosted websites

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Non-HTTP services
docs.heading_path: Use cases > DNS only > Non-HTTP services
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Records used for FTP, SSH, RDP, game servers, or other non-HTTP protocols must be DNS-only. Cloudflare's proxy only handles HTTP and HTTPS traffic. Proxying these records routes the traffic to Cloudflare, which drops the non-HTTP connection.

docs.title: About
docs.heading_path: About
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Multi-signer DNSSEC consists of two models that allow different authoritative DNS providers to serve the same zone and have DNSSEC enabled at the same time.

docs.title: How it works
docs.heading_path: About > How it works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This is a simplified explanation to give you context and clarify what is involved in a multi-signer DNSSEC setup. For technical details refer to RFC 8901 ↗. To read more about DNSSEC, refer to How DNSSEC works ↗.

docs.title: Model 1
docs.heading_path: About > How it works > Model 1
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Whereas in both models all providers have each other's Zone Signing Keys (ZSK) added to their DNSKEY record set, in model 1, only one Key Signing Key (KSK) is used to sign such DNSKEY record sets. Management of this KSK and its reference by the DS record (that is, the Secure…

docs.title: Model 2
docs.heading_path: About > How it works > Model 2
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: In model 2, on the other hand, each provider uses its own KSK to sign its own DNSKEY record set, and these KSKs are then referenced by the DS record (Secure Entry Point).

docs.title: What happens when multi-signer DNSSEC is on
docs.heading_path: About > What happens when multi-signer DNSSEC is on
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. **Internal flag**: Cloudflare sets an internal flag that allows you to add DNSKEY records to your zone. 2. **External ZSKs included**: When you add DNSKEY records from your secondary provider, Cloudflare includes them in the DNSKEY RRset. 3. **Signing with Cloudflare's KSK**:…

docs.title: Best practices

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When setting up multi-signer DNSSEC, follow the best practices below to help you achieve a smooth deployment.

docs.title: Use model 2
docs.heading_path: About > Best practices > Use model 2
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare recommends model 2 for multi-signer setups. In this model, each provider has their own KSK DNSKEY, resulting in two DS records (one for each provider). This provides better independence and flexibility.

docs.title: Understand DNSKEY flags
docs.heading_path: About > Best practices > Understand DNSKEY flags
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When exchanging keys between providers, ensure you are adding the correct key type (typically ZSKs) to the DNSKEY RRset.

docs.title: Adhere to TTLs
docs.heading_path: About > Best practices > Adhere to TTLs
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Always wait for the TTL duration after making changes to DNSKEYs and DS records before proceeding to the next step. This ensures that cached records expire before new records take effect, preventing validation failures.

docs.title: How does DNS Firewall choose a backend nameserver to query upstream?
docs.heading_path: DNS Firewall FAQ > How does DNS Firewall choose a backend nameserver to query upstream?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: DNS Firewall alternates between a customer's nameservers, using an algorithm that is more likely to send queries to the faster upstream nameservers than slower nameservers.

docs.title: How long does DNS Firewall cache a stale object?
docs.heading_path: DNS Firewall FAQ > How long does DNS Firewall cache a stale object?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: As long as there is enough allocated memory, Cloudflare does not clear items from the cache forcefully, even when the TTL expires. This feature allows Cloudflare to serve stale objects from cache if your nameservers are offline.

docs.title: Does the DNS Firewall cache SERVFAIL?
docs.heading_path: DNS Firewall FAQ > Does the DNS Firewall cache SERVFAIL?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes. SERVFAIL is treated like any other negative answer for caching purposes. The default TTL is 30 seconds. You can set a different negative cache TTL on your cluster in the Cloudflare dashboard, or via the API (negative_cache_ttl parameter).

docs.title: Does DNS Firewall support EDNS Client Subnet (ECS)?
docs.heading_path: DNS Firewall FAQ > Does DNS Firewall support EDNS Client Subnet (ECS)?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes. Often, DNS providers want to see a client's IP via EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) (RFC 7871 ↗) because they serve geographically specific DNS answers based on the client's IP. With EDNS Client Subnet enabled, the DNS Firewall will forward the client's IP subnet along with the DNS…

docs.title: Does DNS Firewall cache negative answers?
docs.heading_path: DNS Firewall FAQ > Does DNS Firewall cache negative answers?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes. The default TTL is 30 seconds. You can configure the negative cache TTL on your cluster in the Cloudflare dashboard, or via the API (negative_cache_ttl parameter). This will affect the TTL of responses with status REFUSED, NXDOMAIN, or SERVFAIL.

docs.snippet: At your DNS servers, update the A/AAAA records for your nameserver hostnames in your DNS zone file with your DNS Firewall cluster IP addresses.

docs.title: General DNS issues
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: In web browsers such as Safari or Chrome, there are several commonly observable DNS errors:

docs.title: Common causes and resolutions
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues > Common causes and resolutions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Below are the most common causes for DNS resolution errors along with suggested solutions.

docs.title: Missing DNS records
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues > Common causes and resolutions > Missing DNS records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Ensure that you have the necessary DNS records for the domain or subdomain that is presenting the error.

docs.title: DNSSEC was not disabled before the domain was added to Cloudflare
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues > Common causes and resolutions > DNSSEC was not disabled before the domain was added to Cloudflare
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: DNS resolution failures occur if DNSSEC is not disabled at your domain provider before you add the domain to Cloudflare.

docs.title: Nameservers no longer point to Cloudflare
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues > Common causes and resolutions > Nameservers no longer point to Cloudflare
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you manage DNS records via the Cloudflare dashboard and your domain stops pointing to Cloudflare's nameservers, DNS resolution will stop functioning.

docs.title: Unresolved IP address
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues > Common causes and resolutions > Unresolved IP address
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: In rare cases, the DNS resolver in the client requesting the URL might fail to resolve a DNS record to a valid IP address.

docs.title: Newly created record still does not resolve
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues > Common causes and resolutions > Newly created record still does not resolve
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you recently created a DNS record and resolvers still return NXDOMAIN (Non-Existent Domain) or no answer, it is likely because a negative response is currently stored in the resolver's cache.

docs.title: Further debugging
docs.heading_path: General DNS issues > Common causes and resolutions > Newly created record still does not resolve > Further debugging
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To verify the record was correctly created, query Cloudflare's authoritative nameservers directly:

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.heading_path: Email issues
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you have issues sending or receiving mail, follow these troubleshooting steps.

docs.title: Are your records correct?
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Are your records correct?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To check that your MX records are resolving correctly, run the following dig command in your terminal (replace example.com with your domain):

docs.title: Are DNS records missing?
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Are DNS records missing?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If dig returns no results for your domain's MX records, your records may not have been created or may have been accidentally deleted.

docs.title: Do your MX records point to a delegated subdomain?
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Do your MX records point to a delegated subdomain?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: NS records delegate a subdomain to another DNS provider. If your MX record points to a subdomain that is delegated via NS records (for example, mail.example.com), the mail server records are managed by that external provider, not Cloudflare. Confirm that the external provider…

docs.title: Is CNAME flattening turned on?
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Is CNAME flattening turned on?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Some email providers require CNAME records for features like DKIM authentication or autodiscover. When CNAME flattening is turned on — either globally for all CNAME records or individually on a specific record — the CNAME is flattened to an A record, which can prevent email…

docs.title: Is your mail hostname proxied?
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Is your mail hostname proxied?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Mail protocols such as SMTP, IMAP, and POP3 do not work through Cloudflare's standard HTTP proxy.

docs.title: Common provider record values
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Common provider record values
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you are not sure whether the DNS content itself is correct, compare it with the values from your provider.

docs.title: Is Cloudflare Spectrum turned on?
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Is Cloudflare Spectrum turned on?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare does not proxy email traffic (SMTP, port 25) by default. Unless you have explicitly configured Cloudflare Spectrum to proxy SMTP traffic, email is delivered directly to your mail server and does not pass through the Cloudflare network. DNS records used for email…

docs.title: Is Email Routing turned on?
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Is Email Routing turned on?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If Email Routing is turned on, Cloudflare manages your MX records and may create additional DNS records automatically.

docs.title: Best practices for MX records on Cloudflare
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Best practices for MX records on Cloudflare
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If possible, do not host a mail service on the same server as the web resource you want to protect, since emails sent to non-existent addresses get bounced back to the attacker and reveal the mail server IP address.

docs.title: Contact your mail provider for assistance
docs.heading_path: Email issues > Contact your mail provider for assistance
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If your email does not work shortly after editing DNS records, contact your mail administrator or mail provider with the specific error or bounce message you are receiving. They can confirm whether the issue is with DNS resolution, mail server configuration, or message delivery.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.heading_path: FAQ
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The sections below cover frequently asked questions about Cloudflare authoritative DNS. For DNS Firewall, refer to DNS Firewall FAQ.

docs.title: Is Cloudflare a free DNS (domain nameserver) provider?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Cloudflare offerings > Is Cloudflare a free DNS (domain nameserver) provider?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * You do not need to change your hosting provider to use Cloudflare. * You do not need to move away from your registrar. The only change you make with your registrar is to point the authoritative nameservers to the Cloudflare nameservers.

docs.title: Does Cloudflare charge for or limit DNS queries?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Cloudflare offerings > Does Cloudflare charge for or limit DNS queries?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare never limits or caps DNS queries, but the pricing depends on your plan level.

docs.title: Does Cloudflare offer domain masking?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Cloudflare offerings > Does Cloudflare offer domain masking?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: No. Cloudflare does not offer domain masking or DNS redirect services (your hosting provider might). However, we do offer URL forwarding through Bulk Redirects.

docs.title: Can subdomains be added directly to Cloudflare?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Cloudflare offerings > Can subdomains be added directly to Cloudflare?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes. Enterprise customers can add subdomains directly to Cloudflare via subdomain support.

docs.title: Does Cloudflare support EDNS0 (extension mechanisms for DNS)?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Cloudflare offerings > Does Cloudflare support EDNS0 (extension mechanisms for DNS)?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes, EDNS0 is a building block for modern DNS implementations and is enabled for all Cloudflare customers. EDNS0 adds support for signaling if the DNS Resolver (recursive DNS provider) supports larger message sizes and DNSSEC.

docs.heading_path: FAQ > Nameservers > Where can I find my Cloudflare nameservers?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Also, the IP address associated with a specific Cloudflare nameserver can be retrieved via a dig command or a third-party DNS lookup tool hosted online such as whatsmydns.net ↗:

docs.title: Where do I change my nameservers to point to Cloudflare?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Nameservers > Where do I change my nameservers to point to Cloudflare?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Make the change at your registrar, which is where you registered your domain. This may or may not be your hosting provider - refer to Update nameservers for further context.

docs.title: Why have I received an email: (mydomain) stopped using Cloudflare's nameservers?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Nameservers > Why have I received an email: (mydomain) stopped using Cloudflare's nameservers?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: For domains where Cloudflare hosts the DNS, Cloudflare continuously checks whether the domain uses Cloudflare's nameservers for DNS resolution. If Cloudflare's nameservers are not used, the domain status is updated from **Active** to **Moved** and an email is sent to the…

docs.title: Why does my new zone have different nameservers than my other zones?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Nameservers > Why does my new zone have different nameservers than my other zones?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Nameserver assignments happen at zone creation and cannot be changed afterwards, even by Cloudflare Support.

docs.title: Does Cloudflare limit the number of DNS records a domain can have?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > DNS records > Does Cloudflare limit the number of DNS records a domain can have?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes. Refer to DNS records quota for current limits per plan and details on how quotas are enforced.

docs.title: How long does it take for a DNS change I made to push out?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > DNS records > How long does it take for a DNS change I made to push out?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, any changes or additions you make to your Cloudflare zone file will take effect globally within 5 minutes, usually much less.

docs.title: Why can't I make ANY queries to Cloudflare DNS servers?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > DNS records > Why can't I make ANY queries to Cloudflare DNS servers?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: ANY queries are special and often misunderstood. They are usually used to get all record types available on a DNS name, but what they return is just any type in the cache of recursive resolvers. This can cause confusion when they are used for debugging.

docs.title: How do I add ANAME records on Cloudflare?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > DNS records > How do I add ANAME records on Cloudflare?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: ANAME or ALIAS are DNS records used by specific DNS providers. If your previous provider was using ANAME or ALIAS, you can recreate these records on Cloudflare as CNAME records. Cloudflare's CNAME flattening1 allows you to create CNAME records at your zone apex, removing the…

docs.heading_path: Public buckets
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Public Bucket is a feature that allows users to expose the contents of their R2 buckets directly to the Internet. By default, buckets are never publicly accessible and will always require explicit user permission to enable.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Domain access through a custom domain allows you to use Cloudflare Cache to accelerate access to your R2 bucket.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Disabling a domain will turn off public access to your bucket through that domain. Access through other domains or the managed r2.dev subdomain are unaffected. The specified domain will also remain connected to R2 until you remove it or delete the bucket.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Disable public development URL

docs.title: Storage classes
docs.heading_path: Storage classes
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Storage classes allow you to trade off between the cost of storage and the cost of accessing data. Every object stored in R2 has an associated storage class.

docs.title: Available storage classes
docs.heading_path: Storage classes > Available storage classes
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Available storage classes

docs.title: Standard storage
docs.heading_path: Storage classes > Available storage classes > Standard storage
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Standard storage is designed for data that is accessed frequently. This is the default storage class for new R2 buckets unless otherwise specified.

docs.title: Example use cases
docs.heading_path: Storage classes > Available storage classes > Standard storage > Example use cases
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Website and application data * Media content (e.g., images, video) * Storing large datasets for analysis and processing * AI training data * Other workloads involving frequently accessed data

docs.title: Infrequent Access storage
docs.heading_path: Storage classes > Available storage classes > Infrequent Access storage
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Infrequent Access storage is ideal for data that is accessed less frequently. This storage class offers lower storage cost compared to Standard storage, but includes retrieval fees and a 30 day minimum storage duration requirement.

docs.title: Example use cases
docs.heading_path: Storage classes > Available storage classes > Infrequent Access storage > Example use cases
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Long-term data archiving (for example, logs and historical records needed for compliance) * Data backup and disaster recovery * Long tail user-generated content

docs.title: Set default storage class for buckets
docs.heading_path: Storage classes > Set default storage class for buckets
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By setting the default storage class for a bucket, all objects uploaded into the bucket will automatically be assigned the selected storage class unless otherwise specified. Default storage class can be changed after bucket creation in the Dashboard.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To learn more about how to specify the storage class for new objects, refer to the Workers API and S3 API documentation.

docs.title: Upload objects
docs.heading_path: Upload objects
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: There are several ways to upload objects to R2\. Which approach you choose depends on the size of your objects and your performance requirements.

docs.title: Choose an upload method
docs.heading_path: Upload objects > Choose an upload method
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Most S3-compatible SDKs and tools (such as rclone) automatically choose multipart upload for large files based on a configurable threshold. You do not typically need to implement multipart logic yourself when using the S3 API.

docs.title: Upload via dashboard
docs.heading_path: Upload objects > Upload via dashboard
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the **R2 object storage** page.  Go to **Overview** ↗ 2. Select your bucket. 3. Select **Upload**. 4. Drag and drop your file into the upload area or **select from computer**.

docs.title: Create a folder
docs.heading_path: Upload objects > Upload via dashboard > Create a folder
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can also create folders from the dashboard by selecting **Create folder**. This creates a zero-byte object with a key ending in / that acts as a placeholder. For more information on how folders work in R2, refer to Prefixes and folders.

docs.title: Upload via Workers API
docs.heading_path: Upload objects > Upload via Workers API
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Use R2 bindings in Workers to upload objects server-side. Refer to Use R2 from Workers for instructions on setting up an R2 binding.

docs.heading_path: Upload objects > Upload via Workers API > Single upload

docs.snippet: Use put() to upload an object in a single request. This is the simplest approach for small to medium objects.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Use createMultipartUpload() and resumeMultipartUpload() for large files or when you need to upload parts in parallel. Each part must be at least 5 MiB (except the last part).

docs.title: Temporary credentials
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Temporary credentials are short-lived, scoped S3 credentials derived from an existing R2 API token. They authenticate with AWS Signature Version 4, the same as a long-lived token, but include a session token and expire automatically. The session token is sent with every request…

docs.title: Choosing an approach
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Choosing an approach
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: R2 supports two patterns for time-limited access. They overlap but have different trade-offs:

docs.title: Via the Temporary Credentials API
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Generate temporary credentials > Via the Temporary Credentials API
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The Temporary Credentials API accepts a parent API token, the bucket name, and optional scoping parameters, and returns a new access key ID, secret access key, and session token. Cloudflare signs the session token on your behalf.

docs.title: Locally (client-side signing)
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Generate temporary credentials > Locally (client-side signing)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can also generate temporary credentials locally by signing a JWT with your parent API token's secret access key and using it as the session token.

docs.title: Scope of a credential
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Scope of a credential
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Every temporary credential is bound to a single bucket and a set of permitted operations. You can optionally restrict the credential further to specific paths within the bucket.

docs.title: Bucket
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Scope of a credential > Bucket
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A temporary credential is bound to exactly one bucket, identified by name. Cross-bucket access is not supported within a single credential.

docs.title: Permitted operations
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Scope of a credential > Permitted operations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Specify permitted operations using scope (passed as permission to the API) or actions. You must provide at least one.

docs.title: Scope
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Scope of a credential > Permitted operations > Scope
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: scope is a preset category of operations. Refer to Permissions for full definitions.

docs.title: Actions
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Scope of a credential > Permitted operations > Actions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: For example, actions: ["GetObject", "HeadObject"] grants read of individual objects but denies ListObjectsV2, even though the broader object-read-only scope would allow listing.

docs.title: Paths
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Scope of a credential > Paths
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Restrict access to specific prefixes or objects within the bucket. Omit these fields to grant access to the entire bucket, subject to the permitted operations.

docs.title: Using temporary credentials
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Using temporary credentials
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Any S3-compatible client that supports session tokens will accept R2 temporary credentials. Pass all three values (access key ID, secret access key, session token) using the client's standard credential fields.

docs.title: Security considerations
docs.heading_path: Temporary credentials > Security considerations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Treat temporary credentials as bearer tokens. Anyone in possession of all three values can perform the allowed operations until the credential expires.

docs.title: What are Durable Objects?
docs.heading_path: What are Durable Objects?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A Durable Object is a special kind of Cloudflare Worker which uniquely combines compute with storage. Like a Worker, a Durable Object is automatically provisioned geographically close to where it is first requested, starts up quickly when needed, and shuts down when idle. You…

docs.title: Durable Objects highlights
docs.heading_path: What are Durable Objects? > Durable Objects highlights
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Durable Objects have properties that make them a great fit for distributed stateful scalable applications.

docs.title: In-memory state
docs.heading_path: What are Durable Objects? > Durable Objects features > In-memory state
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Each Durable Object has its own in-memory state. Applications can use this in-memory state to optimize the performance of their applications by keeping important information in-memory, thereby avoiding the need to access the durable storage at all.

docs.title: Storage API
docs.heading_path: What are Durable Objects? > Durable Objects features > Storage API
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The Durable Object Storage API allows Durable Objects to access fast, transactional, and strongly consistent storage. A Durable Object's attached storage is private to its unique instance and cannot be accessed by other objects.

docs.title: Alarms API
docs.heading_path: What are Durable Objects? > Durable Objects features > Alarms API
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Durable Objects provide an Alarms API which allows you to schedule the Durable Object to be woken up at a time in the future. This is useful when you want to do certain work periodically, or at some specific point in time, without having to manually manage infrastructure such as…

docs.title: WebSockets
docs.heading_path: What are Durable Objects? > Durable Objects features > WebSockets
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: WebSockets are long-lived TCP connections that enable bi-directional, real-time communication between client and server. Because WebSocket sessions are long-lived, applications commonly use Durable Objects to accept either the client or server connection.

docs.title: RPC
docs.heading_path: What are Durable Objects? > Durable Objects features > RPC
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Durable Objects support Workers Remote-Procedure-Call (RPC) which allows applications to use JavaScript-native methods and objects to communicate between Workers and Durable Objects.

docs.title: Does an empty table / SQLite database contribute to my storage?
docs.heading_path: FAQs > Pricing > Does an empty table / SQLite database contribute to my storage?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Yes, although minimal. Empty tables can consume at least a few kilobytes, based on the number of columns (table width) in the table. An empty SQLite database consumes approximately 12 KB of storage.

docs.heading_path: FAQs > Pricing > Does metadata stored in Durable Objects count towards my storage?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: All writes to a SQLite-backed Durable Object stores nominal amounts of metadata in internal tables in the Durable Object, which counts towards your billable storage.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Durable Objects can scale horizontally across many Durable Objects. Each individual Object is inherently single-threaded.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Durable Objects are designed such that the number of individual objects in the system do not need to be limited, and can scale horizontally.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.heading_path: Getting started
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare Queues is a flexible messaging queue that allows you to queue messages for asynchronous processing. By following this guide, you will create your first queue, a Worker to publish messages to that queue, and a consumer Worker to consume messages from that queue.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.heading_path: Getting started > Prerequisites
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Use a Node version manager like Volta ↗ or nvm ↗ to avoid permission issues and change Node.js versions. Wrangler, discussed later in this guide, requires a Node version of 16.17.0 or later.

docs.title: 1\. Create a Worker project
docs.heading_path: Getting started > 1\. Create a Worker project
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You will access your queue from a Worker, the producer Worker. You must create at least one producer Worker to publish messages onto your queue. If you are using R2 Bucket Event Notifications, then you do not need a producer Worker.

docs.title: 2\. Create a queue
docs.heading_path: Getting started > 2\. Create a queue
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To use queues, you need to create at least one queue to publish messages to and consume messages from.

docs.title: 3\. Set up your producer Worker
docs.heading_path: Getting started > 3\. Set up your producer Worker
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To expose your queue to the code inside your Worker, you need to connect your queue to your Worker by creating a binding. Bindings allow your Worker to access resources, such as Queues, on the Cloudflare developer platform.

docs.snippet: When configuring a consumer Worker for a queue, you can also define how messages are batched as they are delivered.

docs.snippet: The following batch-level settings can be configured to adjust how Queues delivers batches to your configured consumer.

docs.title: Explicit acknowledgement and retries
docs.heading_path: Batching, Retries and Delays > Explicit acknowledgement and retries
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can acknowledge individual messages within a batch by explicitly acknowledging each message as it is processed. Messages that are explicitly acknowledged will not be re-delivered, even if your queue consumer fails on a subsequent message and/or fails to return successfully…

docs.title: Delivery failure
docs.heading_path: Batching, Retries and Delays > Delivery failure
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When a message is failed to be delivered, the default behaviour is to retry delivery three times before marking the delivery as failed. You can set max_retries (defaults to 3) when configuring your consumer, but in most cases we recommend leaving this as the default.

docs.title: Delay messages
docs.heading_path: Batching, Retries and Delays > Delay messages
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When publishing messages to a queue, or when marking a message or batch for retry, you can choose to delay messages from being processed for a period of time.

docs.title: Delay on send

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To delay a message or batch of messages when sending to a queue, you can provide a delaySeconds parameter when sending a message.

docs.title: If there is a global delay configured on the queue, ignore it.

docs.title: Consumer concurrency
docs.heading_path: Consumer concurrency
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Consumer concurrency allows a consumer Worker processing messages from a queue to automatically scale out horizontally to keep up with the rate that messages are being written to a queue.

docs.title: Enable concurrency
docs.heading_path: Consumer concurrency > Enable concurrency
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, all queues have concurrency enabled. Queue consumers will automatically scale up to the maximum concurrent invocations as needed to manage a queue's backlog and/or error rates.

docs.title: How concurrency works
docs.heading_path: Consumer concurrency > How concurrency works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: After processing a batch of messages, Queues will check to see if the number of concurrent consumers should be adjusted. The number of concurrent consumers invoked for a queue will autoscale based on several factors, including:

docs.title: Example
docs.heading_path: Consumer concurrency > How concurrency works > Example
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you are writing 100 messages/second to a queue with a single concurrent consumer that takes 5 seconds to process a batch of 100 messages, the number of messages in-flight will continue to grow at a rate faster than your consumer can keep up.

docs.title: Why are my consumers not autoscaling?
docs.heading_path: Consumer concurrency > How concurrency works > Why are my consumers not autoscaling?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * max_concurrency has been set to 1. * Your consumer Worker is returning errors rather than processing messages. Inspect your consumer to make sure it is healthy. * A batch of messages is being processed. Queues checks if it should autoscale consumers only after processing an…

docs.title: Limit concurrency

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare recommends leaving the maximum concurrency unset, which will allow your queue consumer to scale up as much as possible. Setting a fixed number means that your consumer will only ever scale up to that maximum, even as Queues increases the maximum supported invocations…

docs.title: Billing
docs.heading_path: Consumer concurrency > Billing
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When multiple consumer Workers are invoked, each Worker invocation incurs CPU time costs.

docs.title: Example
docs.heading_path: Consumer concurrency > Billing > Example
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A consumer Worker that takes 2 seconds to process a batch of messages will incur the same overall costs to process 50 million (50,000,000) messages, whether it does so concurrently (faster) or individually (slower).

docs.snippet: A pull-based consumer allows you to pull from a queue over HTTP from any environment and/or programming language outside of Cloudflare Workers. A pull-based consumer can be useful when your message consumption rate is limited by upstream infrastructure or long-running tasks.

docs.title: How to choose between push or pull consumer

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Deciding whether to configure a push-based consumer or a pull-based consumer will depend on how you are using your queues, as well as the configuration of infrastructure upstream from your queue consumer.

docs.title: 1\. Enable HTTP pull

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can enable HTTP pull or change a queue from push-based to pull-based via the wrangler CLI or via the Cloudflare dashboard ↗. Enabling HTTP pull from a Wrangler configuration file is no longer supported.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can enable a pull-based consumer on any existing queue by using the wrangler queues consumer http sub-commands and providing a queue name.

docs.title: 2\. Consumer authentication

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: HTTP Pull consumers require an API token with the com.cloudflare.api.account.queues_read and com.cloudflare.api.account.queues_write permissions.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To pull a message, make a HTTP POST request to the Queues REST API with a JSON-encoded body that optionally specifies a visibility_timeout and a batch_size, or an empty JSON object ({}):

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Pull consumers follow a "short polling" approach: if there are messages available to be delivered, Queues will return a response immediately with messages up to the configured batch_size. If there are no messages to deliver, Queues will return an empty response. Queues does not…

docs.title: POST /accounts/${CF_ACCOUNT_ID}/queues/${QUEUE_ID}/messages/pull with the timeout & batch size
docs.heading_path: POST /accounts/${CF_ACCOUNT_ID}/queues/${QUEUE_ID}/messages/pull with the timeout & batch size
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The lease_id allows your pull consumer to explicitly acknowledge some, none or all messages in the batch or mark them for retry. If messages are not acknowledged or marked for retry by the consumer, then they will be marked for re-delivery once the visibility_timeout is reached.…

docs.title: Concurrent consumers
docs.heading_path: POST /accounts/${CF_ACCOUNT_ID}/queues/${QUEUE_ID}/messages/pull with the timeout & batch size > Concurrent consumers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You may have multiple HTTP clients pulling from the same queue concurrently: each client will receive a unique batch of messages and retain the "lease" on those messages up until the visibility_timeout expires, or until those messages are marked for retry.

docs.title: How Queues Works
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare Queues is a flexible messaging queue that allows you to queue messages for asynchronous processing. Message queues are great at decoupling components of applications, like the checkout and order fulfillment services for an e-commerce site. Decoupled services are…

docs.title: What is a queue
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > What is a queue
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A queue is a buffer or list that automatically scales as messages are written to it, and allows a consumer Worker to pull messages from that same queue.

docs.title: Producers
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > Producers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A producer is the term for a client that is publishing or producing messages on to a queue. A producer is configured by binding a queue to a Worker and writing messages to the queue by calling that binding.

docs.title: Content types
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > Producers > Content types
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Messages published to a queue can be published in different formats, depending on what interoperability is needed with your consumer. The default content type is json, which means that any object that can be passed to JSON.stringify() will be accepted.

docs.title: Consumers
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > Consumers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. A consumer Worker, which is push-based: the Worker is invoked when the queue has messages to deliver. 2. A HTTP pull consumer, which is pull-based: the consumer calls the queue endpoint over HTTP to receive and then acknowledge messages.

docs.title: Create a consumer Worker
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > Consumers > Create a consumer Worker
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A consumer is the term for a client that is subscribing to or _consuming_ messages from a queue. In its most basic form, a consumer is defined by creating a queue handler in a Worker:

docs.title: Remove a consumer
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > Consumers > Remove a consumer
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To remove a queue from your project, run wrangler queues consumer remove <queue-name> <script-name> and then remove the desired queue below the [[queues.consumers]] in Wrangler file.

docs.title: Pull consumers
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > Consumers > Pull consumers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A queue can have a HTTP-based consumer that pulls from the queue, instead of messages being pushed to a Worker.

docs.title: Messages
docs.heading_path: How Queues Works > Messages
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Any JSON serializable object can be published to a queue. For most developers, this means either simple strings or JSON objects. You can explicitly set the content type when sending a message.

docs.title: Create indexes
docs.heading_path: Create indexes
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Indexes are the "atom" of Vectorize. Vectors are inserted into an index and enable you to query the index for similar vectors for a given input vector.

docs.snippet: Vectorize V2 requires wrangler version 3.71.0 or later. Ensure you have the latest version of wrangler installed, or use npx wrangler@latest vectorize to always use the latest version.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Dimensions are determined from the output size of the machine learning (ML) model used to generate them, and are a function of how the model encodes and describes features into a vector embedding.

docs.title: Insert vectors
docs.heading_path: Insert vectors
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Vectorize indexes allow you to insert vectors at any point: Vectorize will optimize the index behind the scenes to ensure that vector search remains efficient, even as new vectors are added or existing vectors updated.

docs.title: Supported vector formats
docs.heading_path: Insert vectors > Supported vector formats
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * An array of floating point numbers (converted into a JavaScript number[] array). * A Float32Array ↗ * A Float64Array ↗

docs.title: Metadata
docs.heading_path: Insert vectors > Metadata
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Metadata is an optional set of key-value pairs that can be attached to a vector on insert or upsert, and allows you to embed or co-locate data about the vector itself.

docs.title: Performance Tips When Filtering by Metadata
docs.heading_path: Insert vectors > Metadata > Performance Tips When Filtering by Metadata
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When creating metadata indexes for a large Vectorize index, we encourage users to think ahead and plan how they will query for vectors with filters on this metadata.

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.heading_path: Insert vectors > Namespaces
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Namespaces provide a way to segment the vectors within your index. For example, by customer, merchant or store ID.

docs.title: Improve Write Throughput
docs.heading_path: Insert vectors > Improve Write Throughput
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: One way to reduce the time to make updates visible in queries is to batch more vectors into fewer requests. This is important for write-heavy workloads. To see how many vectors you can write in a single request, please refer to the Limits page.

docs.title: Workers API
docs.heading_path: Insert vectors > Examples > Workers API
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Use the insert() and upsert() methods available on an index from within a Cloudflare Worker to insert vectors into the current index.

docs.heading_path: Insert vectors > Examples > wrangler CLI
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Please use a maximum of 5000 vectors per embeddings.ndjson file to prevent the global rate limit for the Cloudflare API.

docs.title: List vectors
docs.heading_path: List vectors
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The list-vectors operation allows you to enumerate all vector identifiers in a Vectorize index using paginated requests. This guide covers best practices for efficiently using this operation.

docs.title: When to use list-vectors
docs.heading_path: List vectors > When to use list-vectors
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * **Bulk operations**: To process all vectors in an index * **Auditing**: To verify the contents of your index or generate reports * **Data migration**: To move vectors between indexes or systems * **Cleanup operations**: To identify and remove outdated vectors

docs.title: Snapshot consistency
docs.heading_path: List vectors > Pagination behavior > Snapshot consistency
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Vector identifiers returned belong to the index snapshot captured at the time of the first list-vectors request. This ensures consistent pagination even when the index is being modified during iteration:

docs.title: Starting a new iteration
docs.heading_path: List vectors > Pagination behavior > Starting a new iteration
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To see recently added or removed vectors, you must start a new list-vectors request sequence (without a cursor). This captures a fresh snapshot of the index.

docs.title: Response structure
docs.heading_path: List vectors > Pagination behavior > Response structure
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * count: Number of vectors returned in this response * totalCount: Total number of vectors in the index * isTruncated: Whether there are more vectors available * nextCursor: Cursor for the next page (null if no more results) * cursorExpirationTimestamp: Timestamp of when the…

docs.title: Cursor expiration
docs.heading_path: List vectors > Pagination behavior > Cursor expiration
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cursors have an expiration timestamp. If a cursor expires, you'll need to start a new list-vectors request sequence to continue pagination.

docs.title: Performance considerations
docs.heading_path: List vectors > Performance considerations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Take care to have sufficient gap between consecutive requests to avoid hitting rate-limits.

docs.title: Query vectors
docs.heading_path: Query vectors
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Querying an index, or vector search, enables you to search an index by providing an input vector and returning the nearest vectors based on the configured distance metric.

docs.title: Example query
docs.heading_path: Query vectors > Example query
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To pass a vector as a query to an index, use the query() method on the index itself.

docs.title: Query by vector identifier
docs.heading_path: Query vectors > Query by vector identifier
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Vectorize now offers the ability to search for vectors similar to a vector that is already present in the index using the queryById() operation. This can be considered as a single operation that combines the getById() and the query() operation.

docs.title: Control over scoring precision and query accuracy

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When querying vectors, you can specify to either use high-precision scoring, thereby increasing the precision of the query matches scores as well as the accuracy of the query results, or use approximate scoring for faster response times. Using approximate scoring, returned…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. Sign up for a Cloudflare account ↗ if you have not already. 2. Install npm ↗. 3. Install Node.js ↗. Use a Node version manager like Volta ↗ or nvm ↗ to avoid permission issues and change Node.js versions. Wrangler requires a Node version of 16.17.0 or later.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A vector database is distinct from a traditional SQL or NoSQL database. A vector database is designed to store vector embeddings, which are representations of data, but not the original data itself.

docs.snippet: You must create a binding for your Worker to connect to your Vectorize index. Bindings allow your Workers to access resources, like Vectorize or R2, from Cloudflare Workers. You create bindings by updating your Wrangler file.

docs.snippet: Before you deploy your embedding example, ensure your Worker uses your model catalog, including the text embedding model built-in.

docs.title: Vector databases
docs.heading_path: Vector databases
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Vector databases are a key part of building scalable AI-powered applications. Vector databases provide long term memory, on top of an existing machine learning model.

docs.title: Why is a vector database useful?
docs.heading_path: Vector databases > Why is a vector database useful?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A vector database determines what other data (represented as vectors) is near your input query. This allows you to build different use-cases on top of a vector database, including:

docs.title: Vector search
docs.heading_path: Vector databases > Why is a vector database useful? > Vector search
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: In a traditional vector search use-case, queries are made against a vector database by passing it a query vector, and having the vector database return a configurable list of vectors with the shortest distance ("most similar") to the query vector.

docs.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation
docs.heading_path: Vector databases > Why is a vector database useful? > Retrieval Augmented Generation
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is an approach used to improve the context provided to an LLM (Large Language Model) in generative AI use-cases, including chatbot and general question-answer applications. The vector database is used to enhance the prompt passed to the LLM…

docs.title: Databases and indexes
docs.heading_path: Vector databases > Terminology > Databases and indexes
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: In Vectorize, a database and an index are the same concept. Each index you create is separate from other indexes you create. Vectorize automatically manages optimizing and re-generating the index for you when you insert new data.

docs.title: Vector Embeddings
docs.heading_path: Vector databases > Terminology > Vector Embeddings
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Vector embeddings represent the features of a machine learning model as a numerical vector (array of numbers). They are a one-way representation that encodes how a machine learning model understands the input(s) provided to it, based on how the model was originally trained and…

docs.title: Dimensions
docs.heading_path: Vector databases > Terminology > Dimensions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Vector dimensions describe the width of a vector embedding. The width of a vector embedding is the number of floating point elements that comprise a given vector.

docs.title: Distance metrics
docs.heading_path: Vector databases > Terminology > Distance metrics
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The distance metric is an index used for vector search. It defines how it determines how close your query vector is to other vectors within the index.

docs.title: Debugging Pages
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When setting up your Pages project, you may encounter various errors that prevent you from successfully deploying your site. This guide gives an overview of some common errors and solutions.

docs.title: Check your build log
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Check your build log
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the **Workers & Pages** page.  Go to **Workers & Pages** ↗ 2. Select your Pages project. 3. Go to **Deployments** \> **View details** \> **Build log**.

docs.title: Initializing build environment
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Check your build log > Initializing build environment
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Possible errors in this step could be caused by improper installation during Git integration.

docs.title: Cloning git repository
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Check your build log > Cloning git repository
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Possible errors in this step could be caused by lack of Git Large File Storage (LFS). Check your LFS usage by referring to the GitHub ↗ and GitLab ↗ documentation.

docs.title: Building application
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Check your build log > Building application
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Possible errors in this step could be caused by faulty setup in your Pages project. Review your build command, output folder and environment variables for any incorrect configuration.

docs.title: Deploying to Cloudflare's global network
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Check your build log > Deploying to Cloudflare's global network
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.snippet: If your custom domain has not moved from the **Verifying** stage in the Cloudflare dashboard, refer to the following debugging steps.

docs.title: Blocked HTTP validation
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Domain stuck in verification > Blocked HTTP validation
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Pages uses HTTP validation and needs to hit an HTTP endpoint during validation. If another Cloudflare product is in the way (such as Access, a redirect, a Worker, etc.), validation cannot be completed.

docs.title: Missing CAA records
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Domain stuck in verification > Missing CAA records
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If nothing is blocking the HTTP validation, then you may be missing Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) records. This is likely if you have disabled Universal SSL or use an external provider.

docs.title: Zone holds
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Domain stuck in verification > Zone holds
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A zone hold will prevent Pages from adding a custom domain for a hostname under a zone hold.

docs.title: Missing `index.html` on the root `pages.dev` URL
docs.heading_path: Debugging Pages > Domain stuck in verification > Missing `index.html` on the root `pages.dev` URL
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you see a 404 error on the root pages.dev URL (example.pages.dev), you are likely missing an index.html file in your project.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you need additional guidance on build errors, contact your Cloudflare account team (Enterprise) or refer to the Support Center for guidance on contacting Cloudflare Support.

docs.snippet: Cloudflare has taken numerous steps to ensure your security and the integrity of your data in China. Your identification information such as email addresses, password hashes, and billing information are never stored on Cloudflare China Network or shared with the Cloudflare…

docs.title: Does Cloudflare have an MIIT license to provide CDN services in China?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Compliance > Does Cloudflare have an MIIT license to provide CDN services in China?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: As a US company, Cloudflare does not have a license from China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT). However, Cloudflare's partner JD Cloud has all the licenses required by the MIIT to operate and provide CDN services in China.

docs.title: Can Cloudflare or JD Cloud help me to get the ICP?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Compliance > Can Cloudflare or JD Cloud help me to get the ICP?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: No, neither Cloudflare nor JD Cloud is responsible for ICP (Internet Content Provider) applications. However, Cloudflare can help provide referrals to ICP partners specialized in ICP applications. For more information, refer to Obtain an ICP number.

docs.title: Why is my ICP filing/license revoked?
docs.heading_path: FAQ > Compliance > Why is my ICP filing/license revoked?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The application and revocation of ICP filings or licenses is managed by China's local authorities. Usually, either the customer or the agency processing the ICP application will receive a notification with more details. Cloudflare cannot provide the ICP revocation reasons.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > TCP connection failed > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This typically occurs when there is a network failure between Cloudflare and your origin, and/or a firewall refuses to allow our connection. Ensure your network and firewall configurations are not interfering with traffic.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > HTTP timeout occurred > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The origin failed to return an HTTP response within the timeout configured. This happens if you have the timeout set to a low number. For example, one to two seconds.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > Response code mismatch error > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare receives an HTTP status code that does not match the values defined in the expected_codes property of your Health Check configuration.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > Response code mismatch error > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Response codes must match the expected_codes. Confirm the values are correct by comparing the expected response codes and the status code received in the Event Log.

docs.title: ​​Alternate cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > Response code mismatch error > ​​Alternate cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You may also see this issue if you have a Health Check configured to use HTTP connections and your origin server is redirecting to HTTPS. In this case, the response code will often be 301, 302, or 303.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > Response code mismatch error > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Change your Cloudflare Health Check configuration to use HTTPS or set the value of follow_redirect to true so that Cloudflare can resolve the correct status code.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > Response body mismatch error > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The response body returns from your origin server and does not include the (case-insensitive) value of expected_body configured in your Health Check.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > TLS untrusted certificate error > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you’re using a self-signed certificate, Cloudflare recommends either using a publicly trusted certificate or setting the allow_insecure property on your Health Check to true.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > TLS name mismatch error > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Our Health Check (client) was not able to match a name on the server certificate to the hostname of the request.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > TLS name mismatch error > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Inspect your Health Check configuration to confirm that the header value set in the Cloudflare Health Check is correct.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > TLS protocol error > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This error can occur if you are using an older version of TLS or your origin server is not configured for HTTPS.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > TLS unrecognized name error > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The server did not recognize the name provided by the client. When a host header is set, this is set as the ServerName in the initial TLS handshake. If it is not set, Cloudflare will not provide a ServerName, which can cause this error.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > ​​No route to host error > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The IP address cannot be reached from Cloudflare’s network. Common causes are ISP or hosting provider network issues (e.g. BGP level), or that the IP does not exist.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > TCP Timeout > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Confirm whether the SYN-ACK for the handshake takes place at your origin and contact Cloudflare support.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > ​​Network Unreachable > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare cannot connect to the origin web server due to network unavailability. This is usually caused by a network issue or incorrect origin IP.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > ​​Network Unreachable > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Check the IP entered for the origin in Cloudflare’s Health Checks configuration or the IP returned via DNS for the origin hostname.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > HTTP Invalid Response > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Ensure the origin web server responds to requests and that no applications have crashed or are under high load.

docs.title: Cause
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > ​​DNS Internal > Cause
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The origin web server's hostname resolves to a non-publicly-routable or restricted IP address (for example, a localhost address). No checks are run against this origin.

docs.title: Solution
docs.heading_path: Health Checks Analytics > Common error codes > ​​DNS Internal > Solution
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Confirm the origin web server hostname resolves to a publicly routable IP address. Note that if the hostname resolves to a public Cloudflare anycast IP (because the hostname is proxied through Cloudflare), the health check will run but will probe Cloudflare's edge rather than…
