docs.title: Concepts
docs.heading_path: Concepts
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: This page defines and articulates key concepts that are relevant to Cloudflare SSL/TLS and are used in this documentation. For more concepts and broader descriptions, check out the Cloudflare Learning Center ↗.

docs.title: SSL/TLS certificate
docs.heading_path: Concepts > SSL/TLS certificate
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: An SSL/TLS certificate is what enables websites and applications to establish secure connections. With SSL/TLS, a client - such as a browser - can verify the authenticity and integrity of the server it is connecting with, and use encryption to exchange information.

docs.title: Edge certificate
docs.heading_path: Concepts > SSL/TLS certificate > Edge certificate
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The edge certificates are the ones that Cloudflare presents to clients visiting your website or application. You can manage edge certificates through the Cloudflare Dashboard ↗.

docs.title: Origin certificate
docs.heading_path: Concepts > SSL/TLS certificate > Origin certificate
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Origin certificates guarantee the security and authentication on the other side of the network, between Cloudflare and the origin server of your website or application. Origin certificates are managed on your origin server.

docs.title: Validity period
docs.heading_path: Concepts > Validity period
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: One common aspect of every SSL/TLS certificate is that they must have a fixed expiration date. If a certificate is expired, clients - such as your visitor's browser - will consider that a secure connection cannot be established, resulting in warnings or errors.

docs.title: Certificate authority (CA)
docs.heading_path: Concepts > Certificate authority (CA)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: A certificate authority (CA) is a trusted third party that generates and gives out SSL/TLS certificates. The CA digitally signs the certificates with their own private key, allowing client devices - such as your visitor's browser - to verify that the certificate is trustworthy.

docs.title: Validation level
docs.heading_path: Concepts > Validation level
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: SSL/TLS certificates vary in terms of the level to which a CA has validated them. As explained in the article about types of certificates ↗, SSL/TLS certificates can be DV (Domain Validated), OV (Organization Validated) or EV (Extended Validation).

docs.title: Origin pull
docs.heading_path: Concepts > Origin pull
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When visitors request content from your website or application, Cloudflare first attempts to serve content from the cache ↗. If this attempt fails, Cloudflare sends a request back to your origin web server to get the content. This request between Cloudflare and your origin web…

docs.title: Cipher suites
docs.heading_path: Concepts > Cipher suites
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Besides the authentication and integrity aspects that valid certificates guarantee, the other important aspect of SSL/TLS certificates is encryption. Cipher suites determine the set of algorithms that can be used for encryption/decryption and that will be negotiated during an…

docs.title: Trust store
docs.heading_path: Concepts > Trust store
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The list of certificate authority (CA) and intermediate certificates that are trusted by operating systems, web browsers or other software that interacts with SSL/TLS certificates is called trust store. Cloudflare maintains its trust store on a public GitHub repository ↗.

docs.snippet: Depending on your organization requirements, or if you have to troubleshoot an issue with your certificates, for example, you might come across the terms root certificate, intermediate certificate and leaf certificate.

docs.title: DNSLink gateways
docs.heading_path: DNSLink gateways
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When you set up a gateway with a DNSLink record, that gateway is restricted to a particular piece of content — either a specific Content Identifier (CID) or an Interplanetary Name Service (IPNS) hostname. This is called a restricted gateway.

docs.title: What is DNSLink?
docs.heading_path: DNSLink gateways > What is DNSLink?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Every file on IPFS is identified by a CID ↗ — a long string like bafybeiaysi4s6lnjev27ln5icwm6tueaw2vdykrtjkwiphwekaywqhcjze. These CIDs are not practical for end users to type or remember, the same way IP addresses (192.0.2.1) are not practical compared to domain names…

docs.title: How is it used with Cloudflare?
docs.heading_path: DNSLink gateways > How is it used with Cloudflare?
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You have the option to specify the DNSLink when you create an IPFS gateway, which serves as a custom hostname that directs users to a website already hosted on IPFS.

docs.title: Interplanetary File System (IPFS)
docs.heading_path: Interplanetary File System (IPFS)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The Interplanetary File System (IPFS) is a peer-to-peer file storage network. Instead of storing files on a single server (the way traditional web hosting works), IPFS distributes files across many computers around the world.

docs.title: Content Identifiers
docs.heading_path: Interplanetary File System (IPFS) > Content Identifiers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Every file added to IPFS is given a unique address derived from a hash of the file's content. This address is called a Content Identifier (CID). A CID contains two pieces of information: the hash of the file and an identifier for the hash algorithm used, combined into a single…

docs.title: Uploading to IPFS
docs.heading_path: Interplanetary File System (IPFS) > Uploading to IPFS
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: IPFS tracks which computers have which files using a Distributed Hash Table (DHT) ↗ — a lookup system that maps CIDs to the network addresses of computers hosting that content. No single computer holds the entire lookup table. Instead, each computer in the network stores a…

docs.heading_path: Interplanetary File System (IPFS) > Directories
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can upload more than just individual files. For example, consider a folder called example, which has exactly one file, example_text.txt, containing the string I'm trying out IPFS.

docs.title: Get started with API Shield
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: API Shield protects your APIs by discovering endpoints, validating request schemas, and detecting abuse patterns. This guide walks through the initial setup from configuring session identifiers to enabling advanced protections.

docs.title: Session identifiers
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Session identifiers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: While not strictly required, it is recommended that you configure your session identifiers when getting started with API Shield. When Cloudflare inspects your API traffic for individual sessions, we can offer more tools for visibility, management, and control.

docs.title: To set up session identifiers
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Session identifiers > To set up session identifiers
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the **Security Settings** page.  Go to **Settings** ↗ 2. Filter by **API abuse**. 3. On **Session identifiers**, select **Configure session identifiers**. 4. Select **Manage identifiers**. 5. Choose the type of session identifier (cookie,…

docs.title: Create a Schema Profile
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Create a Schema Profile
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Application Profiles provides one Schema Profile with two sources. Schema Learning derives a profile from traffic, while Schema Validation uses an uploaded OpenAPI schema.

docs.title: Enable the Sensitive Data Detection ruleset and accompanying rules
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Enable the Sensitive Data Detection ruleset and accompanying rules
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: API Shield works with the Cloudflare WAF Sensitive Data Detection ruleset to identify API endpoints that return sensitive data, such as social security or credit card numbers, in their HTTP responses. Review these endpoints to verify that sensitive data is only returned where…

docs.title: Manage operations
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Manage operations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Web Assets continuously discovers operations from traffic. An operation represents an endpoint by HTTP method, hostname pattern, and path pattern.

docs.title: Add rate limits to your most sensitive endpoints
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Add rate limits to your most sensitive endpoints
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Rate limiting rules allow you to define rate limits for requests matching an expression, and choose the action to perform when those rate limits are reached.

docs.title: Export a learned schema
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Export a learned schema
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Learned schemas include the hostname, all endpoints by host, method, and path, and detected path variables (for example, /users/{id}). They can also include detected query parameters and their format. You can optionally include rate limit threshold recommendations.

docs.title: View and configure Sequence Analytics
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > View and configure Sequence Analytics
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Sequence Analytics identifies common patterns of API requests — for example, a user checking their account balance before initiating a funds transfer.

docs.title: Set up JSON Web Tokens (JWT) validation
docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Additional configuration > Set up JSON Web Tokens (JWT) validation
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: JSON Web Tokens (JWT) validation verifies that tokens sent by clients have not been tampered with and have not expired. Configure JWT validation using the Cloudflare dashboard or API.

docs.heading_path: Get started with API Shield > Additional configuration > Set up GraphQL malicious query protection
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If your origin uses GraphQL, you may consider setting limits on GraphQL query size and depth.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: API Discovery requires an active API Shield subscription at both the account and zone level. If your subscription is active at the account level but not assigned to the zone, Discovery will not run for that zone.

docs.title: 1\. Activate client-side resource monitoring
docs.heading_path: Get started with client-side security > 1\. Activate client-side resource monitoring
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the Security **Settings** page.  Go to **Settings** ↗ 2. (Optional) Filter by **Client-side abuse**. 3. Turn on **Continuous script monitoring**.

docs.title: 2\. Review detected resources
docs.heading_path: Get started with client-side security > 2\. Review detected resources
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When you enable client-side resource monitoring, it may take a while to get the list of detected scripts in your domain.

docs.title: 3\. (Optional) Configure alerts
docs.heading_path: Get started with client-side security > 3\. (Optional) Configure alerts
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Once you have activated client-side security's resource monitoring, you can set up one or more alerts informing you of relevant client-side changes on your zones. The available alert types depend on your Cloudflare plan and subscriptions.

docs.title: 4\. (Optional) Define content security rules
docs.heading_path: Get started with client-side security > 4\. (Optional) Define content security rules
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Content security rules (previously called policies) define allowed resources on your websites. Create content security rules to implement a positive security model1.

docs.title: 4.1\. Create a content security rule with the Log action
docs.heading_path: Get started with client-side security > 4\. (Optional) Define content security rules > 4.1\. Create a content security rule with the Log action
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: When you create a content security rule with the _Log_ action, Cloudflare logs any resources not covered by the rule, without blocking any resources. Use this action to validate a new rule before deploying it.

docs.title: 4.2\. Review rule violations
docs.heading_path: Get started with client-side security > 4\. (Optional) Define content security rules > 4.2\. Review rule violations
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Resources not covered by the content security rule you created will be reported as rule violations. After some time, review the list of rule violations to make sure the rule is correct.

docs.title: 4.3\. Change rule action to Allow
docs.heading_path: Get started with client-side security > 4\. (Optional) Define content security rules > 4.3\. Change rule action to Allow
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Once you have verified that your content security rule is correct, change the rule action from _Log_ to _Allow_.

docs.snippet: 1. A positive security model is one that defines what is allowed and rejects everything else. In contrast, a negative security model defines what will be rejected and accepts the rest. ↩

docs.title: Precursor
docs.heading_path: Precursor
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Precursor is a client-side, session-based verification system that continuously evaluates a visitor's behavior over time. Instead of relying on a single challenge event, Precursor runs ongoing verification in the browser to detect automation that appears legitimate in individual…

docs.title: How it works
docs.heading_path: Precursor > How it works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * A client-side script is injected into the page * The script continuously collects signals and performs verification * Each execution produces signals that are evaluated by Cloudflare * Results are used to update session state stored in the cf_clearance cookie * The process…

docs.title: Get started
docs.heading_path: Precursor > Get started
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, select your zone. 2. Go to **Security** \> **Settings**. 3. Locate **Precursor**. 4. Turn on Precursor.

docs.title: Precursor Rules (optional)
docs.heading_path: Precursor > Get started > Precursor Rules (optional)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Precursor runs across your zone by default. Precursor Rules do not enable or disable Precursor — they determine which mode applies to each request.

docs.title: Use Precursor with APIs
docs.heading_path: Precursor > Get started > Use Precursor with APIs
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If your zone serves both browser pages and API endpoints, use Precursor Rules to scope where strict enforcement applies.

docs.title: Relationship to JavaScript Detections
docs.heading_path: Precursor > Relationship to JavaScript Detections
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Precursor supersedes JavaScript Detections (JSD). JSD and Precursor both collect client-side signals, but Precursor evaluates them continuously across a session instead of as a one-time check.

docs.title: If you already use JSD
docs.heading_path: Precursor > Relationship to JavaScript Detections > If you already use JSD
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare will disable JSD when you enable Precursor to avoid running both features on the same traffic. Precursor includes all detections previously covered by JSD, and any JSD-driven Security Rules will still apply.

docs.title: If you do not use JSD
docs.heading_path: Precursor > Relationship to JavaScript Detections > If you do not use JSD
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you enable Precursor without previously using JSD, you may see more traffic with bot score below 30.

docs.title: Relationship to Challenge Pages
docs.heading_path: Precursor > Relationship to Challenge Pages
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Challenges provide point-in-time verification * Precursor provides continuous, session-level verification

docs.heading_path: Precursor > Relationship to `cf_clearance` cookie
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * effective clearance may be reduced or invalidated * additional Challenges may be triggered * the visitor may be re-verified during the same session

docs.snippet: Your visitor's HTTP request contains a referer header set to the website that they came from. When they encounter and solve a Challenge Page, the request with the referer is sent to the origin, and the response to the request is served to the user. The JavaScript on the response…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) preflight requests, or OPTIONS, exclude user credentials that include cookies. As a result, the cf_clearance cookie will not be sent with the request, causing it to fail to bypass a Challenge Page (Non-interactive, Managed, or Interactive…

docs.title: Challenges on Cloudflare-protected sites
docs.heading_path: Troubleshooting > Common issues > Challenges on Cloudflare-protected sites
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare issues challenges to website visitors to protect against malicious activity, such as bot attacks and DDoS attempts. If a legitimate human visitor is unexpectedly challenged, the reason typically stems from a security feature flagging their request.

docs.title: Allowlist traffic from mitigation actions
docs.heading_path: Troubleshooting > Common issues > Allowlist traffic from mitigation actions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you need to prevent a **Block** or **Challenge** action from being applied to specific requests, such as known search engine crawlers, monitoring services, or internal APIs, you must configure an exclusion using WAF custom rules.

docs.title: 1\. Use a Skip rule (recommended)
docs.heading_path: Troubleshooting > Common issues > Allowlist traffic from mitigation actions > 1\. Use a Skip rule (recommended)
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The most robust method for creating an exception is to create a custom rule with the **Skip** action. This allows matching requests to bypass certain security features, including Bot Management and other WAF rules.

docs.title: 2\. Modify the Rule Expression
docs.heading_path: Troubleshooting > Common issues > Allowlist traffic from mitigation actions > 2\. Modify the Rule Expression
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can refine the expression of a **Block** or **Challenge** rule to directly exclude known good traffic by using the logical not operator with an exclusion list, such as an IP list, country code, or ASN.

docs.snippet: With a Non-Interactive Challenge, Cloudflare makes the determination on whether or not the visitor is automated based on the limited information attained from their browser signals via an injected JavaScript. Then, it presents a Challenge Page that requires no interaction from a…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Managed Challenges are where Cloudflare dynamically chooses the appropriate type of challenge served to the visitor based on the characteristics of a request from the signals indicated by their browser. This helps avoid CAPTCHAs ↗, which also reduces the lifetimes of human time…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Challenge Pages interrupt the request flow by returning a full HTML page for the user's browser to render and solve. This mechanism fails when the browser expects a non-HTML response, such as an AJAX or XHR (fetch) request.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.snippet: Connect a remote device to a private network so your users can securely access internal applications and services from anywhere, without the security risks and performance bottlenecks of a traditional VPN.

docs.title: How it works
docs.heading_path: Device to network > How it works
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare Tunnel is a network connector that creates an outbound-only connection between your private network and Cloudflare. No open inbound ports or firewall changes are required.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.heading_path: Device to network > Prerequisites
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * A Cloudflare account with a Zero Trust organization. If you have not set this up, refer to Get started. * A Linux, Windows, or macOS device on your private network to run the tunnel. * A Linux, Windows, or macOS device to install the Cloudflare One Client on.

docs.title: Step 1: Assign a Tunnel
docs.heading_path: Device to network > Step 1: Assign a Tunnel
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare Tunnel establishes an outbound connection between your resources and Cloudflare. This is how new devices can reach your private network. You can install Tunnel on any Windows, Mac, or Linux device currently in your private network.

docs.title: Step 2: Set your Tunnel's IP range
docs.heading_path: Device to network > Step 2: Set your Tunnel's IP range
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Add the IP range of your private network to the tunnel. This defines which internal resources your remote users can reach. Your tunnel accepts traffic to this range from devices enrolled in your Zero Trust organization.

docs.title: Step 3: Deploy your Tunnel
docs.heading_path: Device to network > Step 3: Deploy your Tunnel
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Install the cloudflared connector on a device in your private network and run the tunnel. This service creates the secure connection between your network and Cloudflare.

docs.title: Step 4: Enroll your devices
docs.heading_path: Device to network > Step 4: Enroll your devices
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Device enrollment controls which users can connect their devices to your private network through Cloudflare. In this step, you register your first device by providing an email address and installing the Cloudflare One Client.

docs.title: Step 5: Complete Cloudflare One Client setup
docs.heading_path: Device to network > Step 5: Complete Cloudflare One Client setup
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: On your device, complete the Cloudflare One Client installation wizard. Then connect the Cloudflare One Client to your Zero Trust organization. For comprehensive OS-specific instructions, refer to Manual deployment.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify your connection
docs.heading_path: Device to network > Step 6: Verify your connection
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The dashboard confirms that you are securely connected. You now have remote access between your device and your private network resources.

docs.title: How it works

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cloudflare Mesh (formerly WARP Connector) lets you deploy mesh nodes — lightweight network connectors that you install on a single Linux device in each network. That device handles traffic for the entire network: it sends outbound traffic to Cloudflare and receives inbound…

docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * A Cloudflare account ↗. * A Linux device or virtual machine on your first private network. This is where you install your first mesh node. * A second Linux device or virtual machine on a separate private network. This is where you install your second mesh node.

docs.title: Step 1: Create your first mesh node
docs.heading_path: Network to network > Step 1: Create your first mesh node
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to **Networking** \> **Mesh**.  Go to **Mesh** ↗ 2. Select **Add a node**. 3. Enter a name for the node (for example, office-a). 4. Follow the wizard to configure enrollment and device profile settings. 5. Copy the install commands from the…

docs.title: Step 2: Add a route for the first network
docs.heading_path: Network to network > Step 2: Add a route for the first network
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. Go to the node detail page for your first node. 2. Select the **Routes** tab. 3. Select **Add a route**. 4. Enter the IP range of your first network (for example, 10.0.0.0/24). 5. Select **Create**.

docs.title: Step 3: Create your second mesh node
docs.heading_path: Network to network > Step 3: Create your second mesh node
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Repeat Step 1 on a Linux device in your second network. Give it a distinct name (for example, office-b).

docs.title: Step 4: Add a route for the second network
docs.heading_path: Network to network > Step 4: Add a route for the second network
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Repeat Step 2 for your second node, entering the IP range of your second network (for example, 192.168.1.0/24). The IP range must not overlap with your first network.

docs.title: Step 5: Forward device traffic
docs.heading_path: Network to network > Step 5: Forward device traffic
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If the mesh node is installed on your network's router (the device that serves as the default gateway), other devices on the network automatically send traffic through it. No additional configuration is needed, and you can skip this step.

docs.title: Step 6: Verify your connection
docs.heading_path: Network to network > Step 6: Verify your connection
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Devices on both networks can now communicate through Cloudflare. To verify connectivity, try reaching a device on the opposite network (for example, ping 192.168.1.100 from a device on your first network).

docs.snippet: With traditional WANs, you have two options for Internet-bound traffic: backhaul it to a central data center for security inspection (adding latency), or break out directly at the branch (bypassing security controls). Cloudflare One eliminates this tradeoff. Traffic from every…

docs.snippet: WAN transformation is not an all-or-nothing change. Most organizations follow an incremental approach, adding capabilities over time while decommissioning legacy infrastructure as each phase proves out.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Set up site-to-site connectivity by establishing IPsec or GRE tunnels from your existing routers, deploying the Cloudflare One Appliance at branch locations, or using Cloudflare Network Interconnect for private connectivity. Your sites communicate through Cloudflare's network,…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Enable Cloudflare Gateway to apply secure web gateway (SWG) policies to Internet-bound traffic from your sites. Add Cloudflare Network Firewall rules to enforce packet-level filtering. Traffic from every site is inspected at the nearest Cloudflare data center — no backhaul…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: As Cloudflare handles routing and security in the cloud, you can begin decommissioning branch firewalls, VPN concentrators, and MPLS circuits. The end state is what some call "coffee shop networking" — every location, whether a corporate office, a home office, or a coffee shop,…

docs.snippet: Sampling ↗ is a technique used in analytics to analyze a subset of data rather than processing every individual data point. In Cloudflare Analytics, sampling ensures efficient performance and scalability while maintaining high accuracy and reliability. This document provides a…

docs.snippet: We use a sampling method called Adaptive Bit Rate (ABR) ↗ to ensure that queries complete quickly, even when working with large datasets. ABR dynamically adjusts the level of detail in the data retrieved based on query complexity and duration. This approach ensures fairness by…

docs.snippet: Cloudflare's data pipeline handles over 700 million events per second ↗ (and growing) across its global network. Processing and storing all this data in real-time would be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming. By leveraging carefully designed sampling methods, Cloudflare…

docs.snippet: Sampled data is highly reliable, and can provide insights that are as dependable as those derived from full datasets. Cloudflare designs sampling techniques to ensure we capture the essential characteristics of the entire dataset, delivering results you can trust.

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To filter based on the type of data associated with one of the Network Analytics stats, use the **Filter** and **Exclude** buttons that display when you hover over the stat.

docs.snippet: Enable the **Show annotations** toggle to show or hide annotations for advertised/withdrawn IP prefix events in the **Network Analytics** view. Select each annotation to get more details.

docs.title: View logged or monitored traffic
docs.heading_path: Adjust the displayed data > View logged or monitored traffic
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Network DDoS managed rules and Advanced DDoS Protection systems provide a log or monitoring mode that does not drop traffic. These log and monitoring mode events are based on **Verdict** and **Outcome**/**Action** fields.

docs.title: Update payment methods
docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Update payment methods
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You may receive the error message "Your account is limited to 2 payment methods, and you've reached that limit. Please remove an existing payment method before adding a new one." when trying to add additional methods.

docs.title: Supported payment methods
docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Update payment methods > Supported payment methods
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Cards (Visa, Mastercard, American Express, Discover, UnionPay) * PayPal * Apple Pay * Google Pay * Link * Instant Bank Payments via Link (US-based self-serve accounts)

docs.title: 3D Secure authentication
docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Update payment methods > 3D Secure authentication
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Cards issued in regions where 3D Secure is required — for example, the EU under PSD2 or India under RBI — trigger an authentication step with the card issuer. Complete the challenge to save the card.

docs.title: Delete a payment method
docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Delete a payment method
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Before removing your payment method from file, you must cancel all Cloudflare paid services.

docs.title: Update your billing address
docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Update your billing address
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Updating the billing profile address applies to invoices issued after the change. Past invoices keep the address that was on file when they were issued. Updating the billing profile address does not change the address stored on existing payment methods.

docs.title: Update billing email address
docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Update billing email address
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Your billing email address is particularly important if you have opted in to invoice emails.

docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Add or change a Tax ID, VAT, or GST number
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: If you added a payment method but did not include a Tax ID, VAT, or GST number, you can add or change the Tax ID, VAT, or GST number associated with the payment method afterwards.

docs.title: Remove a Tax ID, VAT, or GST number
docs.heading_path: Update billing information > Remove a Tax ID, VAT, or GST number
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You cannot remove a VAT or GST number from past invoices. Removing a VAT or GST number will only apply to future invoices issued in the account.

docs.title: Monitor billable usage
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The billable usage dashboard gives you daily visibility into usage-based costs across your Cloudflare account. The data comes from the same system that generates your monthly invoice, so the figures match your bill.

docs.title: Access the dashboard
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Access the dashboard
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. Log in to the Cloudflare dashboard ↗ and select your account. 2. Go to **Manage Account** \> **Billing**.  Go to **Billing** ↗ 3. Select **Billable Usage**.

docs.title: Cost breakdown chart
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Cost breakdown chart
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The bar chart at the top of the dashboard displays your daily usage charges for the selected billing period. Each bar is stacked by product, so you can identify which products are driving spend and when spending patterns change.

docs.title: Product usage table
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Product usage table
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Below the chart, a sortable table breaks down usage by product for the full billing period.

docs.title: Filter usage by product family or product
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Filter usage by product family or product
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * **Product family** — Group products by family (for example, Workers or R2) to compare costs across related usage metrics. * **Product** — Filter to specific usage metrics. The list of available products narrows based on the families you select.

docs.title: Select a billing period
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Select a billing period
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: By default, the dashboard shows data for your current billing period. Use the date picker to view a previous billing period.

docs.title: Switch between subscriptions
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Switch between subscriptions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: In rare cases, an account has more than one usage-based subscription — usually because a previous subscription was replaced. If this applies to your account, a **Subscription** filter appears in the sidebar, with each subscription labeled by its start date.

docs.title: Data alignment with your invoice
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Data alignment with your invoice
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The dashboard reads from the same data source that generates your monthly invoice.

docs.title: Set up budget alerts
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Set up budget alerts
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To get notified when your spend crosses a dollar threshold, you can create budget alerts directly from the dashboard. For detailed instructions, refer to Budget alerts.

docs.title: Related resources
docs.heading_path: Monitor billable usage > Related resources
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Budget alerts — Get notified when spend crosses a threshold * Usage-based billing — Which products use metered billing * How charges accrue — How a request generates charges across products

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh

docs.title: Log Search
docs.heading_path: Log Search
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Log Explorer enables you to store and explore your Cloudflare logs directly within the Cloudflare dashboard or API, giving you visibility into your logs without the need to forward them to third-party services. Logs are stored on Cloudflare's global network using the R2 object…

docs.title: When to use Log Explorer
docs.heading_path: Log Search > When to use Log Explorer
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Use Log Explorer when you need to investigate what actually happened with real production traffic:

docs.title: Use Log Explorer
docs.heading_path: Log Search > Use Log Explorer
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: 1. In the Cloudflare dashboard, go to the **Log Explorer** \> **Log Search** page.  Go to **Log search** ↗ 2. Select the **Dataset** you want to use and in **Columns** select the dataset fields. If you selected a zone scoped dataset, select the zone you would like to use. 3.…

docs.title: Headers and cookies
docs.heading_path: Log Search > Use Log Explorer > Headers and cookies
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: To query request headers, response headers, and cookies you must first enable logging for these fields using Custom fields. Configure the list of custom fields using the API or the dashboard; there is no need to modify the Logpush job itself.

docs.title: Save queries
docs.heading_path: Log Search > Use Log Explorer > Save queries
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: After selecting all the fields for your query, you can save it by selecting **Save query**. Provide a name and description to help identify it later. To view your saved and recent queries, select **Queries** — they will appear in a side panel where you can insert a new query, or…

docs.title: Integration with Security Analytics
docs.heading_path: Log Search > Integration with Security Analytics
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can also access the Log Explorer dashboard directly from the Security Analytics dashboard. When doing so, the filters you applied in Security Analytics will automatically carry over to your query in Log Explorer.

docs.title: Optimize your queries
docs.heading_path: Log Search > Optimize your queries
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: All the tables supported by Log Explorer contain a special column called date, which helps to narrow down the amount of data that is scanned to respond to your query, resulting in faster query response times. The value of date must be in the form of YYYY-MM-DD. For example, to…

docs.title: Additional query optimization tips
docs.heading_path: Log Search > Optimize your queries > Additional query optimization tips
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Narrow your query time frame. Focus on a smaller time window to reduce the volume of data processed. This helps avoid querying excessive amounts of data and speeds up response times. * Omit ORDER BY and LIMIT clauses. These clauses can slow down queries, especially when…

docs.title: Functions
docs.heading_path: SQL queries supported > Functions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Log Explorer supports a range of SQL functions to transform, evaluate, or summarize data. These include scalar and aggregation functions.

docs.title: Scalar functions
docs.heading_path: SQL queries supported > Functions > Scalar functions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * ARRAY_CONTAINS(array, element) – Checks if the array contains the element.  Example  ARRAY_CONTAINS(['US', 'CA'], ClientCountry)  Returns rows where ClientCountry is either US or CA. * SUBSTRING(string, from_number, for_number) – Extracts part of a string.  Example …

docs.title: Aggregation functions
docs.heading_path: SQL queries supported > Functions > Aggregation functions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * SUM(expression) – Total of values.  Example  SUM(ClientRequestBytes)  Adds up the total number of bytes requested by clients. * MIN(expression) – Minimum value.  Example  MIN(OriginResponseDurationMs)  Finds the shortest response time from origin servers. * MAX(expression) –…

docs.title: Expressions
docs.heading_path: SQL queries supported > Expressions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * CASE WHEN – Conditional logic (like if-else). * AS – Alias for columns or tables. * LIKE – Pattern matching. * IN (list) – Checks if a value is in a list. * BETWEEN ... AND ... – Checks if a value is within a range. * Unary operator – Operates on one operand (for example, -5).…

docs.title: Binary Operators
docs.heading_path: SQL queries supported > Binary Operators
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * Arithmetic: +, -, *, /, % (modulo) * Comparison: >, <, >=, <=, =, != (or <>)\ * Logical: AND, OR, XOR * Bitwise: &, |, ^, >>, << * String concat: ||`

docs.title: Example SQL queries
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: The following examples show practical SQL queries you can use with the http_requests dataset in Log Explorer. For the full list of supported SQL syntax, refer to SQL queries supported.

docs.title: Summarize CDN usage
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries > Summarize CDN usage
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Get a high-level summary of total requests and data transfer for a specific time period. Results include total bytes transferred and conversions to megabytes and gigabytes.

docs.title: Review distribution of security actions
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries > Review distribution of security actions
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Understand how security actions, such as blocks and challenges, are distributed across your traffic and identify the most common security responses applied to requests.

docs.title: Find IPs that triggered challenges
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries > Find IPs that triggered challenges
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Identify the top client IP addresses and request URIs that triggered managed, JavaScript, or interactive challenges to investigate potential bot activity or targeted attacks.

docs.title: Find highest bandwidth consumers by URI
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries > Find highest bandwidth consumers by URI
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Identify which request URIs consume the most bandwidth to pinpoint large assets or endpoints that drive the most data transfer.

docs.title: Analyze client round-trip time by country
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries > Analyze client round-trip time by country
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Analyze client TCP round-trip time (RTT) across different countries to identify regions with high latency that might benefit from additional optimization.

docs.title: Summarize CDN traffic by cache status
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries > Summarize CDN traffic by cache status
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Break down traffic by cache status and measure the average time to first byte (TTFB) for each status to evaluate cache effectiveness and identify opportunities to improve cache hit ratios.

docs.title: Find slowest paths by time to first byte
docs.heading_path: Example SQL queries > Find slowest paths by time to first byte
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Find request paths with the highest average time to first byte (TTFB), along with request counts and server error counts toidentify slow endpoints that may need optimization.

docs.snippet: Use **Select fields** to control which data points Log Explorer stores. Fields are grouped by category, and each category shows its selected field count. Select a category to add or remove all fields in that group, or expand the category to select individual fields. Each field…

docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Deleting a dataset permanently removes the dataset and its stored data. Deletion runs asynchronously. You cannot recreate the same dataset for the account or zone while deletion is in progress.

docs.title: Logpush
docs.heading_path: Logpush
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Logpush delivers logs in batches as quickly as possible, with no minimum batch size, potentially delivering files more than once per minute. This capability enables Cloudflare to provide information almost in real time, in smaller file sizes.

docs.title: Estimating log volume
docs.heading_path: Logpush > Estimating log volume
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Before setting up a Logpush job, you can estimate the total volume of data that will be pushed to your destination. The volume depends on your traffic, selected fields, and compression.

docs.title: Quick sizing for HTTP Requests
docs.heading_path: Logpush > Estimating log volume > Quick sizing for HTTP Requests
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * \~100–250 bytes per request (compressed, depending on fields selected) * 1M requests/day → \~100–250 MB/day * 30M requests/month → \~3–7.5 GB/month

docs.title: Daily storage by traffic volume
docs.heading_path: Logpush > Estimating log volume > Daily storage by traffic volume
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: * 100k req/day → \~25–50 MB/day * 1M req/day → \~250–500 MB/day * 10M req/day → \~2.5–5 GB/day * 100M req/day → \~25–50 GB/day

docs.title: Limits
docs.heading_path: Logpush > Limits
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: There is currently a max limit of **4 Logpush jobs per zone**. Trying to create a job once the limit has been reached will result in an error message: creating a new job is not allowed: exceeded max jobs allowed.

docs.title: Availability
docs.heading_path: Logpush > Availability
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Users without an Enterprise plan can still access Workers Trace Events Logpush by subscribing to the Workers Paid plan.

docs.title: Logpush alerts and analytics
docs.heading_path: Logpush alerts and analytics
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Logpush jobs may fail for a few reasons, for instance because the destination is unreachable, because of a change in permissions at the customers’ origin, or because a Logpush job did not complete at least one successful push in the last 24 hour.

docs.title: Enable alerts
docs.heading_path: Logpush alerts and analytics > Enable alerts
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: You can add an alert for **Failing Logpush Job Disabled** via the **Notifications** section of the dashboard. Note that alerts can be configured at the account level and apply to all jobs within an account.

docs.title: Enable Logpush health analytics
docs.heading_path: Logpush alerts and analytics > Enable Logpush health analytics
docs.attribution: © Cloudflare, Inc., CC BY 4.0 — via documesh
docs.snippet: Customers can query Logpush job health metrics via the GraphQL API. The name of the dataset is logpushHealthAdaptiveGroups and the schema can be explored using the GraphQL API.
